lessons.title: Start here: learn with your eyes and your hands
lessons.intro: Photographs first. Small experiments second. Engineering evidence throughout.
lessons.body:
A robot becomes understandable when you can point to each physical part, name what crosses each wire, and predict what should happen before you press Run. This book starts there. It uses real supplier photographs and source-documentation screenshots; numbered buttons on a photograph reveal an explanation. A reference assembly is explicitly labeled when it is not the exact electrical design of our lab.

Reading format. The text, code and quizzes are stored in this file. Photographs and screen recordings load from their credited original websites, so this edition needs an internet connection for those media. Use the image source link when an image is blocked. The companion package includes a local-image builder for your own connected computer.

A learning sequence that produces evidence

  1. Recognize. Find the connector, component or screen panel in a real photograph. Say its name aloud.
  2. Predict. Write what voltage, measurement, motion or screen result you expect.
  3. Build. Follow one small reversible step. Keep motors disconnected until the logic path is proven.
  4. Observe. Compare the result with your prediction. Photograph your actual wiring and record your software version.
  5. Break safely. Unplug a sensor or stop a process in a controlled experiment. Verify the system reports a fault instead of pretending everything is working.
  6. Explain. Give another person the BOM, pin table and evidence. A working copy on their bench is a stronger milestone than finishing a chapter.

Choose the correct track

A computer and ESP32Projects 1-6; add only one sensor at a timeReal wiring photographs, serial logs and supply measurements

Scope and evidence. This is a teaching labbook, not a certification of a finished commercial machine. The standalone numerical tests supplied with it were executed; embedded firmware, ROS, MuJoCo, Isaac and real mechanical assemblies need validation on the specified equipment. Do not treat a source photograph as proof that a new design has been built.

lessons.title: Your first safe workbench
lessons.intro: Make mistakes in small, low-energy experiments, not in a complete moving machine.
lessons.body:
For the first sessions use a low-voltage USB-powered controller, a breadboard, resistors, an LED, a button and a multimeter. Later, add a current-limited motor supply. Keep mains wiring, unprotected battery packs and high-energy actuators outside the beginner path. A disconnected motor is an excellent way to debug software without creating motion.

Digital multimeterMeasures voltage, resistance and continuityRead the input-jack labels, fused current ranges and manual. Learn DC voltage before measuring current.
USB data cablePowers the board and carries programming dataA charge-only cable may power the LED yet produce no serial device.
Breadboard + jumper wiresMakes temporary low-current circuitsUse good spring contacts; loose jumper wires are not product wiring.
Screwdrivers, flush cutters, tweezersAssembly and wire preparationUse the correct screw head and eye protection when trimming leads.
Caliper or rulerMeasures fit and mounting positionsA printed enclosure must fit the actual module, including solder joints and plugs.
Regulated supply for actuatorsProvides motor/servo power separatelySelect voltage and current from the actual actuator and stall requirements; use current limiting and suitable protection.
Soldering station and fume extractionMakes reliable permanent joints laterPractice on spare material. A shiny joint is not proof of electrical continuity.

Before applying power: use this order

  1. Put the board on an insulating surface. Unplug USB and every external supply. Remove loose screws and metal scraps.
  2. Read the model and revision printed on the board. Identify the power input, GND and voltage rating from its documentation.
  3. Check the breadboard contacts with continuity mode while unpowered. Confirm whether each side rail is split.
  4. Trace every wire by its two endpoint labels. Do not trust wire color as evidence of the function.
  5. Check for an accidental direct short between supply and ground. A capacitor may make the resistance reading change briefly; investigate, do not guess.
  6. Power only the controller. Confirm enumeration and a simple serial message. Then disconnect power and add one peripheral.
  7. When motors are introduced, mount them securely, lift wheels clear, keep a reachable power disconnect and test default-disable before sending a motion command.
Meter trap. For a voltage reading, the meter goes across two nodes. For a current reading, it goes in series with the load. Putting the meter in current mode across a power supply can create a short circuit. After measuring current, return the lead to the voltage/resistance jack. Never use continuity mode on a powered circuit.

The bench notebook

Create one page per experiment: date; exact part numbers; power source; wiring photograph; firmware commit; expected result; observed result; failed trials; next change. Label uncertainty directly: "supplier photograph", "measured on my unit", "estimated", or "not tested". This habit prevents impressive-looking but unreliable documentation.

lessons.title: Photo atlas 1: the small parts that make circuits work
lessons.intro: Recognize resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, switches and adjustment controls.
lessons.body:
Small components are not decoration around the processor. They set signal levels, store energy, protect interfaces and switch loads. Identify the body, pins, markings and polarity before learning a schematic symbol.

Resistor: a controlled restriction

A resistor opposes current. In an LED circuit it sets the current; on a digital input it can prevent a floating voltage. Resistance is measured in ohms. With a 3.3 V supply and an assumed 2.0 V red-LED drop, a 220 ohm resistor gives approximately (3.3 - 2.0)/220 = 5.9 mA. The LED drop is an assumption to check, not a universal constant. More resistance means less current.

Ceramic capacitor: a small local energy buffer

A capacitor stores charge. A 100 nF ceramic near a chip helps supply brief current demands through a short local path. It does not replace a correctly rated power supply. The marking 104 means 100,000 pF. A typical small ceramic is non-polar; the electrolytic below is not.

Electrolytic capacitor: more storage, with polarity

Bulk capacitors can reduce some supply disturbances, but their ESR, ripple-current rating, voltage rating and placement matter. The stripe normally marks the negative side. Installing a polarized capacitor backward can cause failure. A large capacitor is not a cure for an undersized servo supply.

ComponentPlain-language jobMistake to avoid
DiodeLets current pass much more easily in one direction than the otherA single diode across a reversible motor is not a universal protection circuit; use a suitable H-bridge design.
NPN transistorUses a small base drive to control a larger collector currentA base resistor and known pinout are required. Do not assume all TO-92 packages share a pin order.
MOSFETA voltage-controlled switch, useful for efficient load switchingGate threshold is not the voltage at which the MOSFET is guaranteed fully on. Check on-resistance at your actual gate drive.
LEDEmits light when forward current flowsIt is not an ordinary diode to connect straight across the power supply. Use a resistor or current driver.
Fuse / resettable fuseLimits the consequences of some overcurrent faultsIt is not a precision current regulator or a complete human-safety system.
Voltage regulatorConverts or stabilizes a supply voltageVIN, output, ground, dropout, heat and current rating all matter. A connector marked 5 V is not automatically an input.

Potentiometer and switch: two kinds of input

A potentiometer has two ends and a moving wiper. Put the ends across a permitted voltage range and read the wiper with an ADC. A button simply opens or closes contacts. A four-leg tactile switch often contains two permanently common pairs: find those pairs with continuity mode before connecting it. Software debounce recognizes one deliberate press rather than several contact bounces.

lessons.title: Photo atlas 2: sensors are different kinds of evidence
lessons.intro: Range, motion, environment, force, current and vision are separate measurement problems.
lessons.body:
A sensor does not directly tell a robot what to do. It returns a measurement with units, timing, noise and failure modes. The useful question is not "Which sensor is best?" but "Which uncertainty must this measurement reduce?"

Sensor familyWhat it observesWhat it does not guarantee
Ultrasonic rangeEcho travel time along an acoustic viewing regionReliable readings from soft fabric, every oblique surface or several nearby simultaneous transmitters
Time-of-flight optical rangeReflected light timing in the specified field of viewA valid result on every dark, transparent, shiny or sunlit target
Scanning lidarDistances in a scan plane or scan patternAn object above or below that plane; glass can be difficult
RGB cameraColors and texture projected into pixelsDepth, physical size or a grasp pose from a bounding box alone
Depth cameraDepth derived by stereo, structured light or ToFCorrect depth on every material, distance or illumination
EncoderShaft or wheel rotationActual ground travel when wheels slip
Limit switchContact at a known mechanical limitContinuous position over the whole travel range

An accelerometer measures specific force, including the effect of gravity in a stationary tilted sensor. A gyroscope measures angular rate. Integrating a biased gyro creates angle drift. The pictured six-axis IMU does not measure geographic heading by itself. For a first test, hold it still, turn it slowly and compare its signed readings with the printed axes. Do not begin with a complicated filter before verifying the axes and units.

Temperature and humidity are useful for environmental monitoring and for explaining sensor drift. Place the sensing region away from heat-generating electronics. CO2 sensing is a different measurement: the pictured SCD41 uses photoacoustic sensing. A VOC-derived "equivalent CO2" estimate should not be reported as a direct interchangeable CO2 measurement.

PIR responds to changes in infrared patterns; a stationary person may not trigger it continuously. An LDR responds to light-dependent resistance; a divider gives an ADC a voltage to measure. Neither device is a camera. The simplest suitable sensor is often more dependable than an unnecessary vision model.

A load cell bends slightly. Strain gauges turn that bend into tiny resistance changes. A bridge circuit produces a small differential voltage and the HX711 amplifies/digitizes it. Calibration converts raw counts into a chosen unit. The mechanical mount is part of the measurement: a beautiful electronics design cannot fix a load path that bypasses the sensor.

Current monitoring explains why a motor starts, stalls, heats or resets a controller. The INA219 measures a shunt voltage; it is not a current limiter. Keep its logic bus separate in your mental model from the high-current load path. Before inserting a monitor, check its shunt, voltage, current and power limits.

Choose a sensor with a seven-question checklist

  1. What quantity and units do I actually need?
  2. What range, resolution and accuracy matter for the task?
  3. How often must the measurement arrive, and how old may it be?
  4. What voltage and electrical interface does this exact module use?
  5. What does an invalid, saturated or disconnected reading look like?
  6. Where will it be mounted, and how will that location distort the measurement?
  7. How will I calibrate and independently verify it?

lessons.title: Photo atlas 3: motors, sound, screens and power
lessons.intro: Understand what is a sensor, what is an actuator and what supplies the energy.
lessons.body:
A brushed DC motor naturally controls rotation speed through voltage/current and load. Its geared output trades speed for torque. Without an encoder you do not know exact shaft position just because you applied a PWM value. PWM is a switching pattern; it is not a guarantee of speed.

A driver is the bridge between a weak logic signal and a power-hungry actuator. An H-bridge can reverse the current through a DC motor. The pictured board is a specific TB6612 breakout, not a generic L298N or a bare chip. Pin naming, standby defaults and safe current limits differ across boards.

A hobby servo contains a motor, gears, position feedback and control electronics. The external command requests a position within its supported travel. The white plastic horn connects that shaft to your mechanism. Center the servo electrically with the horn removed, disconnect power and attach the horn near the intended mechanical midpoint. Do not use the shaft as a lever to force the gears.

Brushed geared motorSmall wheeled roverStall current, encoder feedback, gearbox play
Position hobby servoLightweight pan headSupply transients, travel stops, unknown internal control
Continuous-rotation servoSimple small driveCommand controls direction/speed rather than absolute angle

SolenoidShort linear actuationHeating, inrush, flyback management and pinch points

An OLED is an output display, a microphone is an audio input, an I2S amplifier is an audio output stage, and a passive buzzer is a simple tone device. Voice requires a data path and an acoustic design, not merely connecting "sound components." The MAX98357A speaker output is bridge-tied: neither speaker terminal is GND.

Battery boundary. Begin with regulated wired power. Identifying a pouch cell is not permission to charge it with a generic supply. Cell chemistry, charging method, protection, load sharing, connector polarity and mechanical protection must all match. Do not puncture, compress or solder directly to an unknown cell.

lessons.title: ESP32-S3: identify every important region
lessons.intro: A microcontroller board is a set of connected subsystems, not just a black rectangle.
lessons.body:
Visible partMeaningWhat you do with it
Metal-shielded moduleThe ESP32-S3 module and associated radio/memory hardwareRead its exact printed variant; flash and PSRAM configuration are not identical across versions.
Antenna regionThe radio radiating structureKeep metal, wiring bundles and enclosure walls away according to the antenna guidance.
USB-to-UART connectorProgramming/logging through a bridge chipUse a data cable for the initial serial examples.
Native USB connectorUSB signals connected to the ESP32-S3 itselfUse only with firmware/configuration that supports the intended native USB function.
BOOT and RESET buttonsEnter download mode and restartFor a failed upload, use the documented boot sequence; do not short random pins.
RegulatorConverts the permitted supply to a logic railIt does not make every GPIO 5 V tolerant.
Pin headersBreakouts for power and GPIO signalsWire by printed signal name and confirmed board diagram.
Power/status LEDsSome visual indication of power or software activityA lit LED does not prove a sensor, USB data connection or application is working.

A first USB session, without any external circuit

  1. Inspect the board label and connector labels. Photograph both faces and save the image in your project.
  2. Plug the USB-to-UART port into your computer using a known data cable. Keep other power sources disconnected.
  3. In Linux, compare ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM* before and after connection; absence of a matching device may simply cause the shell to print an error. Check permissions and cable before changing firmware.
  4. Open PlatformIO or Arduino IDE, select the actual ESP32-S3 board profile and the serial port. Compile a minimal program that writes a message.
  5. Upload. Open the serial monitor at 115200 baud. Press RESET. Confirm the same message appears after a fresh reset.
  6. Disconnect power and only then add the LED circuit from Project 1.
The external LED lab intentionally avoids the onboard RGB LED. Onboard addressable LEDs are not controlled like a plain LED, and their GPIO can differ by board revision.

Why this board is not a Raspberry Pi

The ESP32 normally runs firmware close to the hardware. You choose initialization, timing and tasks explicitly. A Raspberry Pi 5 normally runs a Linux operating system with processes, files, drivers and scheduling. You can combine them: the Pi handles images and user interaction; the ESP32 handles bounded, local device behavior. That split does not automatically create hard real-time guarantees.

lessons.title: Raspberry Pi 5: the computer inside a robot
lessons.intro: Learn connectors, booting, cooling, storage and GPIO numbering before running robot software.
lessons.body:
First boot without attaching GPIO devices

  1. Use Raspberry Pi Imager on an existing computer. Select Raspberry Pi 5 and a supported Raspberry Pi OS image. Check the chosen storage device twice: writing an image erases it.
  2. Configure a hostname and a unique user/password. Enable SSH only deliberately. Keep credentials out of screenshots and public repositories.
  3. Write and verify the microSD image, insert it with the board unpowered, then connect a monitor and keyboard if using a desktop workflow.
  4. Connect a suitable power supply. Use appropriate cooling for sustained workloads. Wait for setup to finish rather than repeatedly unplugging it.
  5. Open a terminal. Run uname -a, python3 --version and ip -br address. Write down what each answer tells you.
  6. Shut down from the operating system before removing power. Connect GPIO or camera ribbons only while powered off.

3.3 V supply1Power rail, not GPIO1
Ground6GND
I2C SDA3BCM2 / SDA
I2C SCL5BCM3 / SCL
Do not rotate a pinout in your head. Orient the actual header using the board documentation before counting pins. The table is a name mapping, not a substitute for the manufacturer orientation drawing. Pi GPIO uses 3.3 V logic.

Camera, cooling and storage are physical constraints

A camera ribbon must match the connector width and pin count on both devices. A cable that fits a previous Pi revision may not fit Pi 5. Opening the connector latch is different from pulling the connector off the board. Secure the cable against rubbing and leave a service loop. Mount the camera rigidly: a flexible camera mount changes calibration whenever the robot vibrates.

An enclosure needs airflow and room around plugs. A fast AI model running briefly on an open desk may throttle inside a warm sealed shell. Measure performance in the final enclosure with the intended power source, not only on a developer bench.

lessons.title: Wire literacy: connections you can verify
lessons.intro: Power, signals and protocols must not be mixed together.
lessons.body:
A wire should be documented as endpoint A - endpoint B - signal - allowed voltage - expected behavior. Color is a convenience, not a contract. A good harness can be tested without remembering who assembled it.

// Low-voltage bench scanner; power every breakout from 3.3 V in this lab.
#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Wire.h>
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200); delay(300);
  Wire.begin(8, 9); Wire.setClock(100000);
  Serial.println("I2C scan: SDA=8 SCL=9, 100 kHz");
  unsigned count = 0;
  for (uint8_t address = 8; address < 120; ++address) {
    Wire.beginTransmission(address);
    if (Wire.endTransmission() == 0) {
      Serial.printf("ACK at 0x%02X\n", address); ++count;
    }
  }
  Serial.printf("%u addresses acknowledged. ACK is not a full sensor test.\n", count);
}

lessons.title: Fit, fasten and service: the mechanical lesson
lessons.intro: A beautiful exterior is not useful until the internals fit, move safely and remain repairable.
lessons.body:
These are photographs from a real pan-tilt kit, not renders of a proposed enclosure. Study how a servo case is retained, how a horn transfers motion and how the second axis is supported. Use the source kit instructions for its particular fasteners. A different SG90-shaped servo can have different ears, spline, cable exit and horn dimensions.

Make a measured envelope before designing a shell

MeasureIncludeWhy it matters
Board length/widthHeader overhang and component edge clearanceA PCB outline alone misses the real footprint
Board heightTallest component and solder joints belowA screw or shell can short the underside
Connector spacePlug body plus cable bend and insertion travelA socket can be visible but impossible to use
Moving sweepHorn, linkage, fastener and wire envelopeCable collision can stop the servo or wear insulation
Service routeTool access and removable lidA robot that cannot be opened will be expensive to repair
Thermal routeHeat source, air path and material limitsA closed case changes operating temperature

A practical assembly sequence for a small desk head

  1. Print only a thin fit-check coupon around one mounting hole and connector opening. Measure the real module against it.
  2. Mount electronics on insulating standoffs. Ensure no screw tip touches traces, solder joints or the display back.
  3. Center the unlinked servo using a conservative pulse range. Disconnect power. Install the horn and bracket near the desired midpoint.
  4. Attach the lightweight display or camera carrier. Move it gently through the intended range with power off without forcing gears.
  5. Route a flexible cable loop along the rotation axis where practical. Clamp the stationary end for strain relief; never use a solder joint as the cable anchor.
  6. Set software limits inside the mechanical limits. Test a narrow range with low available energy and immediate power access.
  7. Close the lid only after taking clear top, bottom and side photographs of the actual wiring. Repeat thermal and movement tests with the lid installed.

Cross-section thinking without a fictional cutaway

For your own build, remove the lid and take a real top-down photograph. Label five layers: support/base, power distribution, controller, moving mechanism, cover. For each adjacent pair, record a measured clearance. A drawing can show an intended clearance, but only a measurement proves that your printed parts and hardware actually fit. This book does not present an invented internal render as an as-built photograph.

For a simple static torque estimate, a 0.10 kg head whose centre of mass is 0.04 m from its tilt axis needs about 0.10 x 9.81 x 0.04 = 0.039 N m merely to hold against gravity in the worst orientation. Acceleration, friction, cable drag and uncertain actuator ratings increase the requirement. Reduce mass and move it toward the axis before buying a stronger motor.

lessons.intro: Compatibility is a skill. A reproducible older baseline is better than an undocumented mixture of releases.
lessons.body:
A robotics workstation is a controlled experiment. Keep the operating system, middleware, simulator, GPU driver and Python environment compatible. Do not put every package into one global Python installation. A tutorial written for an older simulator may use a different command name, robot asset format or library API.

The Isaac Sim screenshot in this book is from archived documentation. Use it to recognize panels, not to decide which release to install. Current hardware requirements and compatibility notes are linked below. A screenshot can be authentic and still be from an older release.

Directory structure you can actually maintain

Open the workspace layout text
robotics-lab/
  hardware/       # board photos, pin tables, BOM, measurements
  firmware/       # one build configuration per firmware project
  ros_ws/src/     # ROS packages, not arbitrary pip libraries
  models/         # URDF, SDF, MJCF and USD assets
  experiments/    # dated configurations, logs and videos
  tests/          # repeatable checks and fault-injection cases
  reports/        # results, limitations and decisions
  environment/    # versions and reproducible installation notes

Environment discipline

  1. Create a project directory and initialize Git. Keep secrets and bulky raw recordings out of ordinary commits.
  2. Install only the first required stack. For ROS, use the official Ubuntu installation page and verify the ROS demo before adding a simulator.
  3. Keep ROS system Python separate from unrelated pip environments. A virtual environment can accidentally hide system ROS packages.
  4. For MuJoCo, create a dedicated venv. The provided requirements file pins the tutorial package, not a claim that it is the newest release.
  5. Run the environment-record script. Save the result with your experiment.
  6. Record one working baseline before upgrading anything. Change one dependency layer at a time, rerun the same tests and retain a rollback path.
Read 18_environment_record.py python
Save 18_environment_record.py
"""Record the local environment without installing anything."""
import importlib.metadata,json,platform,subprocess,sys
from pathlib import Path
out={'python':sys.version,'platform':platform.platform(),'packages':{},'commands':{}}
for name in ['mujoco','gymnasium','torch','lerobot','opencv-python','numpy']:
    try:out['packages'][name]=importlib.metadata.version(name)
    except importlib.metadata.PackageNotFoundError:out['packages'][name]='not installed'
for cmd in [['git','--version'],['nvidia-smi','--query-gpu=name,driver_version,memory.total','--format=csv,noheader']]:
    try:
        r=subprocess.run(cmd,capture_output=True,text=True,timeout=10)
        out['commands'][' '.join(cmd)]=(r.stdout or r.stderr).strip()
    except (FileNotFoundError,subprocess.TimeoutExpired) as exc:out['commands'][' '.join(cmd)]=str(exc)
Path('environment.json').write_text(json.dumps(out,indent=2))
print('Saved environment.json. Review before sharing; machine details may be private.')

RViz is an inspection instrument for ROS data. A robot can be simulated elsewhere, or it can be physical, while RViz shows its model, transforms, sensor measurements and planned paths. Orbiting the camera in RViz does not physically turn a robot. That distinction prevents many beginner mistakes.

lessons.intro: The authentic interface is a laboratory instrument. Learn selection, inspection, stepping and reset before autonomy.
lessons.body:
Know the three things you are looking at

Visual geometry is what you see. Collision geometry is what physics uses for contact. Inertial properties describe mass and how difficult it is to rotate a body. An object can look convincing and still have no useful collision shape or a physically unreasonable inertia.

Visible regionUse it forDo not confuse it with
ViewportInspect objects, position the camera, select modelsTraining a learning policy
Entity TreeFind a named model, link, joint or world entityA list of ROS nodes
Component InspectorInspect properties of the selectionA complete robot control panel
Play/pause/stepAdvance or freeze simulation timeStart/stop a separate external controller process

First session: do these actions in order

  1. Install Harmonic using its version-specific documentation. In a terminal check gz sim --versions. Keep the output in your environment notes.
  2. Start with gz sim shapes.sdf when the packaged example is available. Otherwise use the self-contained world in Project 14.
  3. Pause physics. Identify the Entity Tree and select one model by name. Observe the matching selection in the viewport.
  4. Open or locate Component Inspector. Compare the model pose with your visual estimate.
  5. Use the translate tool on the selected object while paused. Observe which coordinate axis moves. Then undo/reset rather than randomly dragging several objects.
  6. Press Play. Watch the time indicator advance. Pause and use a single-step control to separate a fast event into smaller increments.
  7. Reset. Confirm whether world time, model pose and external program state were all reset; they may not be controlled by the same process.
  8. Save the SDF in your project. Reopen it from a clean session and repeat the same experiment.

What a useful simulation record contains

Save the initial pose, mass, collision geometry, friction parameters, timestep, controller configuration and random seed where applicable. Capture both the viewport and the numerical signal you care about. A video alone cannot explain whether a fall came from unstable integration, a controller sign error or an incorrect centre of mass.

A USD stage is a scene description. A prim is an object in that hierarchy. A rigid body can move under physics. A collider participates in collision detection. An articulation connects joints and links into a multibody mechanism. Isaac Lab adds experiment structure, environments, observations, rewards, resets and learning interfaces; it is not merely another skin for the viewport.

Operate the simulator before training

  1. Run the official compatibility checks and review GPU/driver requirements for the release you selected. Do not assume that a gaming GPU or a cloud notebook automatically satisfies them.
  2. Create a fresh project/stage. Identify Stage and Property before adding a complex robot.
  3. Add a ground surface and a simple dynamic rigid object through the documented workflow for that release. Verify collider and rigid-body properties.
  4. Press Play and confirm the object responds to gravity and rests on the ground. Stop/reset.
  5. Select the object in Stage and inspect its transform and physics properties. Change one parameter, save a separate stage and compare.
  6. Add a camera only after basic physics works. Distinguish the viewer camera from a simulated robot sensor that emits images.
  7. Open an example robot articulation from the supported assets. Inspect joint limits and fixed/free base configuration before sending commands.
  8. Keep the simple stage as a debugging baseline. A large photorealistic world is a poor starting point for diagnosing a missing collider.

What an RL training run really looks like

In a typical Isaac Lab experiment, many copies of an environment step together. An algorithm samples observations, chooses actions, receives rewards and updates a policy. The visible robots may be only a subset; headless training can run without a viewport. Watch episode length, reward terms, termination causes, throughput and held-out evaluation. A field of moving robots is not proof that learning is happening.

The linked NVIDIA walkthrough contains a real Cartpole training demonstration. Use it alongside Project 18: first inspect a random/untrained policy, then a saved trained checkpoint, with the same evaluation conditions. Keep the versioned tutorial track separate from newer Isaac Lab launchers.

lessons.intro: A dataset is a physical measurement record. Treat calibration and timing as carefully as model architecture.
lessons.body:
The recording comes from the LeRobot repository. It shows real robotic hardware, but its filename is not a mechanical assembly specification. Use the exact SO-101 guide for the arm you purchase or print. Servo versions, leader/follower roles, bus IDs, calibration procedures and camera mounts are part of the system.

The workflow, in physical order

  1. Identify the exact robot variant and obtain its matching BOM, printable files and assembly guide. Check motor labels and voltage ratings before powering it.
  2. Assemble unpowered. Check joint motion and cable routing without forcing gears. Fix the base to the work surface.
  3. Configure motor IDs as the guide specifies; connecting a whole chain of unconfigured devices can create conflicts.

  6. Teleoperate slowly. Demonstrate the task with consistent start and end conditions, including safe recovery.

Build a visible heartbeat before adding intelligence. A changing light and a repeatable startup log make later faults much easier to isolate.

What you are building

The finished result is a small controller-and-LED bench circuit, not a complete robot. Take your own top-down photograph and annotate GPIO4, resistor, anode, cathode and ground.

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Disconnect all power. Identify GPIO4 and GND by printed name on the board and the official diagram.
  2. Place the resistor and LED on separate breadboard contact groups. Do not put both LED leads into the same internally connected group.
  3. Connect the series path in the table. The resistor may be on either side of the LED electrically; it must remain in series.
  4. Check the LED polarity. The flat package edge and longer lead are clues; the component datasheet and a suitable meter diode test are stronger evidence.
  5. Create the PlatformIO project described in the screen tour. Copy 01_blink_button.cpp into src/main.cpp; leave the button unconnected for this first lab.
  6. Build, upload and open the serial monitor. Observe the external LED for at least ten complete cycles.
  7. Measure the voltage across the resistor while the LED is on. Estimate current with I = V/R, without moving the meter lead into the current jack.
  8. Reset the board. Unplug/reconnect USB. Confirm behavior starts consistently rather than depending on an old application state.

Software and observations

Read 01_blink_button.cpp C++
Save 01_blink_button.cpp
// ESP32-S3; external LED on GPIO4 through 220 ohm to GND.
// Button: GPIO5 to GND; internal pull-up enabled. No motor connected.
#include <Arduino.h>
constexpr int LED = 4, BUTTON = 5;
bool rawOld = HIGH, stable = HIGH, enabled = true, ledState = false;
uint32_t changedAt = 0, blinkAt = 0;
void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP); Serial.begin(115200);
}
void loop() {
  const uint32_t now = millis();
  const bool raw = digitalRead(BUTTON);
  if (raw != rawOld) { rawOld = raw; changedAt = now; }
  if ((uint32_t)(now - changedAt) >= 30 && raw != stable) {
    stable = raw;
    if (stable == LOW) { enabled = !enabled; Serial.println(enabled ? "RUN" : "PAUSE"); }
  }
  if (!enabled) { ledState = false; digitalWrite(LED, LOW); }
  else if ((uint32_t)(now - blinkAt) >= 500) {
    blinkAt = now; ledState = !ledState; digitalWrite(LED, ledState);
  }
}

The first version alternates the LED every 500 ms. setup() runs once after reset; loop() runs repeatedly. The unsigned elapsed-time comparison avoids an ordinary millis() wraparound bug.

lessons.intro: Turn raw electrical contact into a reliable user action. This becomes your robot's push-to-talk or pause button.
lessons.body:
Beginner bench buildProject 02

Turn raw electrical contact into a reliable user action. This becomes your robot's push-to-talk or pause button.

What you are building

The final interaction is a controllable status beacon. You are practicing event semantics: pressed is not the same event as still being held.

Parts / prerequisites

ItemQuantity or requirementPurpose
Project 1 circuitCompletedVisible output
Normally open momentary button1Human input
Jumper wires2Signal and ground

Wire-by-wire / interface contract

FromToMeaning / check
GPIO5One contact of a normally open pairINPUT_PULLUP in firmware
GNDOther switched contactPress creates a LOW input

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Unplug USB. With continuity mode identify which button legs are permanently connected and which connect only when pressed.
  2. Place the switch so the intended two electrical sides are not shorted by the breadboard. A four-leg button can appear correctly placed while bypassing the switch.
  3. Wire GPIO5 to one switched side and GND to the other. No 5 V connection belongs in this circuit.
  4. Use the same 01_blink_button.cpp program. The internal pull-up makes the idle input HIGH; pressing pulls it LOW.
  5. Upload and press once. The LED heartbeat should pause and the serial monitor should print one PAUSE message.
  6. Release and press again. The heartbeat should resume. Hold for five seconds: it should not toggle continuously.
  7. Repeat twenty presses at different speeds. Count intended presses and logged transitions.
  8. Temporarily remove debounce in a copy of the program and observe contact behavior; restore the robust version before integrating it.

Software and observations

The program tracks the raw reading, the last change time and the stable state. A new stable state is accepted only after 30 ms without another edge. That is a teaching value to measure for your switch, not a universal constant.

Make a display show what the system knows, rather than decorating a black box with animated eyes.

What you are building

The photographed board is a physical reference, not a universal pinout. Your completed build should show a simple readable state panel; playful eyes come after state reporting is reliable.

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Read the actual display pin labels. Some OLED boards support SPI or have a different pin order than a four-pin I2C module.
  2. Disconnect power and wire the four connections. Keep wires short.
  3. Run 02_i2c_scan.cpp before the display library. Record the responding address; do not assume every SSD1306 is 0x3C.
  4. Install Adafruit SSD1306, Adafruit GFX Library and their dependencies through your project library configuration.
  5. Copy 03_oled_status.cpp into src/main.cpp and set the detected address. Build and upload.
  6. Observe BENCH READY and an increasing seconds counter. Reset and confirm it starts over.
  7. Change the text to IDLE, LISTENING or OFFLINE in a controlled code change. Use a state variable rather than many scattered drawing calls.

Save 03_oled_status.cpp
// Requires Adafruit SSD1306, Adafruit GFX Library and Adafruit BusIO.
#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>
Adafruit_SSD1306 screen(128, 64, &Wire, -1);
bool ready = false;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200); Wire.begin(8,9); Wire.setClock(100000);
  ready=screen.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC,0x3C); // Confirm address first.
  if (!ready) Serial.println("DISPLAY_INIT_FAILED");
}
void loop() {
  if (!ready) { delay(1000); return; }
  screen.clearDisplay(); screen.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
  screen.setTextSize(1); screen.setCursor(0,0); screen.println("BENCH READY");
  screen.setTextSize(2); screen.setCursor(0,20); screen.print(millis()/1000);
  screen.setTextSize(1); screen.println(" sec"); screen.display(); delay(250);
}

lessons.intro: Build a small desk proximity indicator and learn why invalid measurements must never be silently converted into "clear path."
lessons.body:
Beginner sensor buildProject 04

Build a small desk proximity indicator and learn why invalid measurements must never be silently converted into "clear path."

What you are building

A useful final product is a truthful indicator, not an autonomous safety sensor. The operating range you document belongs to your tested materials and lighting.

Parts / prerequisites

ItemQuantity or requirementPurpose

Ruler and several targetsWhite card, dark fabric, angled surfaceTest conditions

Wire-by-wire / interface contract

FromToMeaning / check

XSHUTLeave as documented for one sensorDo not randomly ground shutdown

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Disconnect power. Wire the sensor on the same I2C bus as the display. Match named pins, not the pictured board orientation.
  2. Keep the optical aperture exposed. Remove only packaging film identified by the vendor; do not scratch the optical package.
  3. Run the scanner. Expect the display address and 0x29 for this single sensor.
  4. Install Adafruit VL53L0X and the display libraries. Load 03_distance_display.cpp.
  5. Hold a flat target at measured positions such as 100, 200 and 400 mm in moderate indoor lighting. Record 30 samples at each distance.
  6. Repeat with dark fabric and an angled reflective target. Note invalid results separately from numerical error.
  7. Change ambient lighting and repeat a small subset. Do not promise a universal range from one good white-card test.
  8. Design your UI so invalid or stale data is unmistakable. Never label an invalid sample zero distance or infinite distance without a defined reason.

Software and observations

Read 03_distance_display.cpp C++
Save 03_distance_display.cpp
// Requires Adafruit SSD1306, Adafruit GFX Library, Adafruit VL53L0X.
// Bench example, not a collision-prevention safety system.
#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>
#include <Adafruit_VL53L0X.h>
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(128, 64, &Wire, -1);
Adafruit_VL53L0X sensor;
constexpr uint8_t OLED_ADDRESS = 0x3C; // Verify with the scanner.
bool displayOK = false, sensorOK = false;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200); Wire.begin(8, 9); Wire.setClock(100000);
  displayOK = display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDRESS);
  sensorOK = sensor.begin(0x29, false, &Wire);
  Serial.printf("display=%d distance_sensor=%d\n", displayOK, sensorOK);
}
void loop() {
  bool valid = false; uint16_t mm = 0;
  if (sensorOK) {
    VL53L0X_RangingMeasurementData_t m;
    sensor.rangingTest(&m, false);
    valid = (m.RangeStatus == 0); mm = m.RangeMilliMeter;
  }
  if (valid) Serial.printf("distance_mm=%u\n", mm);
  else Serial.println("NO_VALID_RANGE");
  if (displayOK) {
    display.clearDisplay(); display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE); display.setCursor(0, 0);
    display.println("DISTANCE BENCH");
    display.setTextSize(2);
    if (valid) { display.print(mm); display.println(" mm"); }
    else display.println("INVALID");
    display.display();
  }
  delay(100);
}

The teaching code accepts RangeStatus == 0 and otherwise prints NO_VALID_RANGE. More sophisticated behavior should follow the sensor API status definitions and your task requirements.

What you are building

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Wire power-off and run the scanner. Disconnect other devices initially to isolate mistakes.
  2. Install the Adafruit LSM6DS library and dependencies. Load 04_imu_logger.cpp.
  3. Set the module on a stable surface. Capture at least several seconds with no movement. Record units and sample timing.
  4. Rotate the board so each marked axis points up in turn. Determine which acceleration component changes sign and magnitude.
  5. Rotate slowly about one axis. Compare the corresponding gyro sign with the coordinate convention.
  6. Compute a static roll estimate with atan2(ay,az), respecting your chosen orientation convention. Compare it with a simple physical angle reference.
  7. Shake or translate the sensor and observe that an accelerometer-only tilt estimate becomes unreliable. Explain why extra acceleration looks like changed gravity direction.
  8. Estimate gyro bias while stationary. Integrate raw rate over time and observe drift; do not claim absolute heading from a six-axis sensor alone.

What you are building

  3. Install the SHT31 library and run 05_climate_logger.cpp. Read the JSON lines.

What you are building

The finished object is a low-energy test scale, not a calibrated legal-for-trade or safety device. The load cell and platform must both remain below their safe load limits.

What you are building

The reference assembly photo below shows a real driver bench with different controller and motor hardware. It is useful for recognizing physical parts, not for copying the electrical connections into this lab.

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Read the exact driver voltage, current and thermal limits. A cheap TT motor can exceed a small driver's current rating when stalled. Do not assume compatibility by motor size.
  2. Mount the motor securely with the wheel clear. Prepare a reachable motor-supply disconnect. Leave motor power OFF.
  3. Wire logic, shared reference and control pins. Keep motor current out of breadboard power rails and controller pins.
  4. Address the onboard STBY pull-up. For this breakout a 1k pull-down against its documented 10k pull-up is one bench approach; calculate the resulting LOW level and verify it against the input threshold. A production design needs a deliberate hardware-enable strategy.
  5. Upload 07_motor_deadman.cpp. With motor supply still off, measure that STBY is LOW at boot/reset and without commands.
  6. Apply current-limited motor power. Confirm no motion. In serial monitor use no line ending and send a single f. Expect only a brief low-duty pulse.
  7. Send x to disable. Stop sending commands and confirm timeout. Test controller reset and USB disconnection while guarding the setup.
  8. Measure actual current and coast/stop behavior. Disable is not the same as instant braking. Do not reverse a spinning load abruptly.

Software and observations

Save 07_motor_deadman.cpp
// Low-power bench example ONLY. Lift the wheel clear of people and cables.
// GPIO15=AIN1, 16=AIN2, 17=PWMA, 18=STBY. External default-disable required.
// Adafruit TB6612 board: add the documented STBY pull-down/gating.
// 'f' refreshes low-speed drive for 250 ms; any other byte stops.
#include <Arduino.h>
constexpr int IN1=15, IN2=16, PWM=17, ENABLE=18;
constexpr uint32_t TIMEOUT_MS = 250;
uint32_t lastCommand = 0; bool armed = false;
void stopMotor() {
  digitalWrite(ENABLE, LOW); analogWrite(PWM, 0);
  digitalWrite(IN1, LOW); digitalWrite(IN2, LOW); armed = false;
}
void setup() {
  const int pins[] = {IN1, IN2, PWM, ENABLE};
  for (int pin : pins) { digitalWrite(pin, LOW); pinMode(pin, OUTPUT); }
  Serial.begin(115200); stopMotor(); Serial.println("DISABLED; send f for a short low-power pulse");
}
void loop() {
  while (Serial.available()) {
    const char c = (char)Serial.read();
    if (c == 'f') { lastCommand = millis(); armed = true; }
    else stopMotor();
  }
  if (armed && (uint32_t)(millis() - lastCommand) < TIMEOUT_MS) {
    digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH); digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
    analogWrite(PWM, 60); digitalWrite(ENABLE, HIGH);
  } else stopMotor();
}
The software timeout is 250 ms in this teaching example. It is not a certified stopping specification. Motor inertia, driver state and load determine actual motion after disable. A 1k pull-down is not a substitute for a risk-assessed safety circuit.

Create a small controllable head for a camera or display. Learn centering, cable clearance, electrical limits and repeatable assembly.

What you are building

These are genuine reference assembly photographs. The supplied firmware controls one initial axis; expanding to a complete desk robot is Project 11. Photograph your own underside and side views before closing an enclosure.

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Lay out the actual kit parts as in the source photo. Compare servo case, mounting ears, shaft and cable exit with the kit drawing.
  2. Keep the horn removed. Connect one unloaded servo to a separate rated supply with common ground.
  3. Install ESP32Servo and load 08_servo_head.cpp. Send c to request a conservative centre pulse. Disconnect power.
  4. Fit the bracket and horn near the intended centre. Use the correct short retaining screw; a too-long screw can damage the servo.
  5. Compare the base, side and bracket-stage photos. Ensure the pivot axis is aligned and screws do not squeeze a freely moving joint.
  6. Attach a very light dummy payload. Check cable slack and movement envelope. Do not force geared motion by hand.
  7. Power at low risk and test the limited 70-110 degree command interval. Use a/d for small changes; x detaches command output.
  8. Only after measuring current and checking limits add the real display/camera. Recheck every connector through the entire intended range.

Software and observations

Read 08_servo_head.cpp C++
Save 08_servo_head.cpp
// Requires ESP32Servo. One unloaded hobby servo only; separate rated 5 V supply.
// Signal=GPIO10. Common signal ground. Start with horn removed.
// Serial: c=center, a=-5 degrees, d=+5 degrees, x=detach.
#include <Arduino.h>
#include <ESP32Servo.h>
Servo head; int target=90, current=90; bool enabled=false;
uint32_t lastStep=0;
void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); Serial.println("Horn OFF. Send c to enable centre pulse."); }
void loop() {
  while (Serial.available()) {
    char c=(char)Serial.read();
    if (c=='x') { head.detach(); enabled=false; }
    if (c=='c') {
      if (!enabled) { head.setPeriodHertz(50); head.attach(10,1000,2000); enabled=true; }
      target=90;
    }
    if (enabled && c=='a') target=max(70,target-5);
    if (enabled && c=='d') target=min(110,target+5);
  }
  if (enabled && (uint32_t)(millis()-lastStep)>=20) {
    lastStep=millis();
    if (current<target) ++current; else if (current>target) --current;
    head.write(current);

"""USB-camera red-target tracker. It NEVER sends motor commands."""
import argparse, time
import cv2
import numpy as np

def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--camera',type=int,default=0)
    parser.add_argument('--min-area',type=float,default=300.0)
    args=parser.parse_args()
    cap=cv2.VideoCapture(args.camera)
    if not cap.isOpened(): raise SystemExit('Camera did not open. Check index, permissions and cable.')
    previous=time.monotonic()
    try:
        while True:
            ok, frame=cap.read()
            if not ok: raise RuntimeError('Camera frame lost; no target/action may be assumed.')
            hsv=cv2.cvtColor(frame,cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
            mask=(cv2.inRange(hsv,np.array([0,100,60]),np.array([10,255,255])) |
                  cv2.inRange(hsv,np.array([170,100,60]),np.array([179,255,255])))
            contours,_=cv2.findContours(mask,cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
            target=max(contours,key=cv2.contourArea) if contours else None
            label='NO TARGET'
            if target is not None and cv2.contourArea(target)>=args.min_area:
                x,y,w,h=cv2.boundingRect(target); cx=x+w/2
                error=(cx-frame.shape[1]/2)/(frame.shape[1]/2)
                cv2.rectangle(frame,(x,y),(x+w,y+h),(0,255,0),2)
                label=f'normalized horizontal error={error:+.2f}'
            now=time.monotonic(); dt=now-previous; previous=now
            cv2.putText(frame,label,(12,30),cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX,0.6,(255,255,255),2)
            cv2.putText(frame,f'frame interval {dt*1000:.1f} ms',(12,58),cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX,0.5,(255,255,255),1)
            cv2.imshow('Real camera - software-only tracking',frame)
            if cv2.waitKey(1)&0xFF in (27,ord('q')): break
    finally:
        cap.release(); cv2.destroyAllWindows()
if __name__=='__main__': main()

Hue wraps around for red in OpenCV's usual 8-bit HSV representation, so the code combines two hue intervals. It is a simple baseline, not a semantic object recognizer. A target bounding box does not yield metric distance.

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Study the source rover photos. They show an older Raspberry Pi/Motor HAT build; use them for chassis recognition, not as the ESP32 electrical plan.
  2. Measure wheel radius and wheel-to-wheel track width. Record loaded dimensions where possible; a soft tire changes its effective radius.

  4. Mount the electronics on standoffs, with accessible power disconnect and strain-relieved cables. Keep loose wires away from wheels.
  5. Test one motor at a time using Project 8 procedures. Then test both with wheels off the floor. Confirm forward signs and independent timeout behavior.
  6. Attach and verify encoders. Rotate a wheel by one full revolution and compare counted edges with the encoder/gear ratio definition.
  7. Define low-speed straight, rotate-in-place and stop tests in a clear enclosed test area. No people or fragile objects belong in the path.
  8. Measure actual distance and heading. Compare commanded and measured motion. A timed pulse is not odometry.
  9. Add closed-loop wheel speed control only after the sign and count tests pass.
  10. Capture your actual underside, top, side and harness photographs. Make a separate wiring diagram for your exact MCU and driver, not the historical reference configuration.

Software and observations

Read 10_control_math.py python
Save 10_control_math.py
"""Standard-library robotics calculations and a deliberately simple dynamic plant."""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import sin,cos,isfinite

def led_resistance(voltage:float,forward_drop:float,current_a:float)->float:
    if not all(map(isfinite,(voltage,forward_drop,current_a))) or current_a<=0 or voltage<=forward_drop:
        raise ValueError('Require finite supply > LED drop and positive current.')
    return (voltage-forward_drop)/current_a

def wheel_speeds(v:float,yaw_rate:float,radius:float,track:float):
    if radius<=0 or track<=0: raise ValueError('Radius and track must be positive.')
    return ((v-yaw_rate*track/2)/radius,(v+yaw_rate*track/2)/radius)

def forward_2link(l1:float,l2:float,q1:float,q2:float):
    if l1<=0 or l2<=0: raise ValueError('Link lengths must be positive.')
    return (l1*cos(q1)+l2*cos(q1+q2),l1*sin(q1)+l2*sin(q1+q2))

def stopping_distance(speed:float,delay_s:float,deceleration:float)->float:
    if speed<0 or delay_s<0 or deceleration<=0: raise ValueError('Invalid motion parameters.')
    return speed*delay_s+speed**2/(2*deceleration)

@dataclass
class PID:
    kp:float=1.5; ki:float=1.0; kd:float=0.0
    limit:float=3.0; integral:float=0.0; previous_error:float=0.0
    def update(self,target:float,measured:float,dt:float)->float:
        if dt<=0: raise ValueError('dt must be positive.')
        e=target-measured
        proposed=self.integral+e*dt
        raw=self.kp*e+self.ki*proposed+self.kd*(e-self.previous_error)/dt
        out=max(-self.limit,min(self.limit,raw))
        # Conditional integration prevents further windup into a saturated direction.
        if abs(raw)<self.limit or (raw>self.limit and e<0) or (raw<-self.limit and e>0):
            self.integral=proposed
        self.previous_error=e
        return out

def response(seconds=6.0,dt=0.01):
    controller=PID(); x=0.0; rows=[]
    for k in range(round(seconds/dt)):
        u=controller.update(1.0,x,dt)
        x += dt*((-x+u)/0.35) # First-order toy plant, not a specific real motor.
        rows.append(((k+1)*dt,x,u))
    return rows

if __name__=='__main__':
    import csv
    with open('pid_response.csv','w',newline='') as f:
        w=csv.writer(f); w.writerow(['time_s','measurement','command']); w.writerows(response())
    print('Wrote pid_response.csv; simulated toy plant, not hardware data.')

Differential drive: v = r(wR + wL)/2 and yaw_rate = r(wR - wL)/L. With r = 0.04 m, L = 0.16 m and v = 0.20 m/s straight ahead, both wheels need 5 rad/s. These are ideal kinematic relationships; slip and compliance remain physical errors.

Simulation/software labProject 14

Create a world whose physics can be checked with a hand calculation. Learn why models need more than a visible mesh.

What you are building

Your final product is a small real simulation experiment with a verifiable result. Do not call a nice render a digital twin until important physical behavior has been calibrated.

Parts / prerequisites

ItemQuantity or requirementPurpose

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Read the supplied SDF. Identify world, model, link, visual, collision, inertial and plugin entries.
  2. Launch gz sim 13_gazebo_world.sdf. The file uses local primitive geometry, avoiding a remote robot-asset dependency.
  3. Before pressing Play, find falling_cube in the Entity Tree and inspect its starting position.
  4. Press Play and watch the cube fall to the floor. Pause and inspect the settled position.
  5. Estimate the free-fall interval from the cube's bottom clearance: t approximately sqrt(2h/g). Do not expect exact visual timing from a manually clicked stopwatch.
  6. Make a copy without the collision element, then another with a different mass. Predict each outcome and compare. Restore the correct model.
  7. Change max_step_size conservatively and compare numerical stability and timing. Keep all other conditions fixed.
  8. Save the model, configuration, screen capture and a one-paragraph explanation of every difference.

Use an exact small model, a torque bound and logged motion to understand dynamics, damping and controller ownership.

What you are building

Build and operate, one step at a time

  1. Use the real MuJoCo viewer tour and official recording in the platform chapter. Pause the recording to identify the viewport, controls and information overlays; then compare them with your local viewer.
  2. Open the MJCF and identify gravity, timestep, hinge axis, rod, bob and actuator limit.
  3. Launch the native viewer to inspect the mechanism. Then run the Python experiment headless to remove rendering from the numerical baseline.

  5. Run with kd = 0, then kd = 0.08 and compare angle/velocity CSVs. Rename the output after each run so you do not overwrite evidence.

  7. Change timestep in a copy of the XML; rerun the same case. Look for numerical differences before making controller claims.

"""MuJoCo 3.x pendulum experiment. Requires mujoco; not run in this workspace."""
import argparse,csv,time
from pathlib import Path

def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser(); p.add_argument('--headless',action='store_true')
    p.add_argument('--seconds',type=float,default=8.0); p.add_argument('--kd',type=float,default=0.08)
    a=p.parse_args()
    if a.seconds<=0 or a.kd<0: raise SystemExit('Use positive duration and nonnegative damping.')
    import mujoco
    model=mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(Path(__file__).with_name('11_mujoco_pendulum.xml')))
    data=mujoco.MjData(model); data.qpos[0]=0.6; mujoco.mj_forward(model,data)
    rows=[]
    def step():
        data.ctrl[0]=max(-0.4,min(0.4,-a.kd*float(data.qvel[0])))
        mujoco.mj_step(model,data)
        rows.append((float(data.time),float(data.qpos[0]),float(data.qvel[0]),float(data.ctrl[0])))
    if a.headless:
        while data.time<a.seconds: step()
    else:
        import mujoco.viewer
        with mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(model,data) as viewer:
            while viewer.is_running() and data.time<a.seconds:
                start=time.monotonic()
                with viewer.lock(): step()
                viewer.sync()
                time.sleep(max(0,model.opt.timestep-(time.monotonic()-start)))
    with open('pendulum.csv','w',newline='') as f:
        w=csv.writer(f); w.writerow(['time_s','angle_rad','velocity_radps','torque_Nm']); w.writerows(rows)
    print('Saved pendulum.csv. In passive mode this Python loop owns stepping; UI pause is not a safety stop.')
if __name__=='__main__': main()

import argparse,csv,time
from pathlib import Path

def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser(); p.add_argument('--headless',action='store_true')
    p.add_argument('--seconds',type=float,default=8.0); p.add_argument('--kd',type=float,default=0.08)
    a=p.parse_args()
    if a.seconds<=0 or a.kd<0: raise SystemExit('Use positive duration and nonnegative damping.')
    import mujoco
    model=mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(Path(__file__).with_name('11_mujoco_pendulum.xml')))
    data=mujoco.MjData(model); data.qpos[0]=0.6; mujoco.mj_forward(model,data)
    rows=[]
    def step():
        data.ctrl[0]=max(-0.4,min(0.4,-a.kd*float(data.qvel[0])))
        mujoco.mj_step(model,data)
        rows.append((float(data.time),float(data.qpos[0]),float(data.qvel[0]),float(data.ctrl[0])))
    if a.headless:
        while data.time<a.seconds: step()
    else:
        import mujoco.viewer
        with mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(model,data) as viewer:
            while viewer.is_running() and data.time<a.seconds:
                start=time.monotonic()
                with viewer.lock(): step()
                viewer.sync()
                time.sleep(max(0,model.opt.timestep-(time.monotonic()-start)))

"""Small, reproducible Q-learning lab. It is NOT a Gazebo/Isaac simulation."""
import argparse,csv,random
SIZE=5; START=(0,0); GOAL=(4,4); BLOCKS={(1,1),(1,2),(3,3)}
ACTIONS=((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1))
def transition(state,action):
    dr,dc=ACTIONS[action]; candidate=(state[0]+dr,state[1]+dc)
    if not (0<=candidate[0]<SIZE and 0<=candidate[1]<SIZE) or candidate in BLOCKS:
        return state,-2.0,False
    return candidate,(20.0 if candidate==GOAL else -1.0),candidate==GOAL

def train(episodes=1500,seed=7):
    rng=random.Random(seed)
    q={(r,c):[0.0]*4 for r in range(SIZE) for c in range(SIZE) if (r,c) not in BLOCKS}
    log=[]
    for ep in range(episodes):
        state=START; total=0; done=False; steps=0
        epsilon=max(0.05,0.8*(1-ep/max(1,episodes)))
        for steps in range(1,101):
            action=rng.randrange(4) if rng.random()<epsilon else max(range(4),key=lambda a:q[state][a])
            nxt,reward,done=transition(state,action)
            target=reward+(0 if done else 0.95*max(q[nxt]))
            q[state][action]+=0.2*(target-q[state][action])
            state=nxt; total+=reward
            if done: break
        log.append((ep,total,steps,done))
    return q,log

def evaluate(q):
    state=START; route=[state]
    for _ in range(100):
        action=max(range(4),key=lambda a:q[state][a]); state,_,done=transition(state,action);route.append(state)
        if done:return route,True
    return route,False
if __name__=='__main__':
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--seed',type=int,default=7);a=p.parse_args()
    q,log=train(seed=a.seed);route,ok=evaluate(q)
    with open('grid_training.csv','w',newline='') as f:
        w=csv.writer(f);w.writerow(['episode','return','steps','success']);w.writerows(log)
    print('Toy-grid greedy evaluation:',ok,'route:',route)

lessons.title: The mathematics you can touch
lessons.intro: Build intuition for units, frames, wheel motion, arm geometry and torque with worked numerical examples.
lessons.body:
Start with measurements rather than a wall of symbols. A robot has a position, a direction, a mass and a limited ability to move. Mathematics gives these observations precise names so that two people can build the same machine. Keep the units next to every number. A correct-looking calculation with centimetres mixed into a metre-based controller is still wrong.

One rotation, explained physically

Stand behind a rover. Its forward direction is one axis; its left direction is another. A point one metre in front of the rover is not necessarily one metre east in the room. A rotation tells you how one observer describes another observer's directions. For planar motion, x points forward, y left and positive yaw turns counter-clockwise when viewed from above under the ROS convention.

xworld = xrobot + cos(θ) xlocal − sin(θ) ylocal
yworld = yrobot + sin(θ) xlocal + cos(θ) ylocal

Worked example. The robot is at (2, 1) m and faces 90 degrees counter-clockwise from the world x axis. A target is 0.5 m directly ahead in its own coordinates. cos(90°) = 0 and sin(90°) = 1, so the target is at (2, 1.5) m. Write that result on paper before plotting it. A point behind the robot should move in the opposite direction.

Why a two-wheeled rover turns

Each wheel pushes its side of the chassis. Equal wheel speeds produce straight motion in an ideal no-slip model. A faster right wheel makes the rover turn left. Let r be wheel radius, L be distance between wheel contact centres and ω be each wheel's angular speed in radians per second.

v = r(ωR + ωL)/2
Ω = r(ωR − ωL)/L

Worked example. r = 0.03 m, L = 0.16 m, right speed = 6 rad/s and left speed = 4 rad/s. Forward speed is 0.15 m/s and yaw rate is 0.375 rad/s. The ideal turn radius is v/Ω = 0.40 m. On a slippery floor this model is a prediction, not a measurement. The test is to compare the predicted arc with an independently measured path.

A small arm: reaching is geometry before AI

x = l1 cos(q1) + l2 cos(q1 + q2)
y = l1 sin(q1) + l2 sin(q1 + q2)

Two 0.10 m links with q1 = 0 and q2 = 90 degrees put the tip at (0.10, 0.10) m. Forward kinematics starts with angles and finds the tip. Inverse kinematics starts with a desired tip and finds possible angles. There can be no solution, several solutions, or a configuration where a tiny desired movement requires a large joint change. Joint limits and collision checks eliminate many mathematically possible answers.

Torque is not the same thing as speed

Holding a 0.05 kg payload 0.08 m horizontally from a joint requires roughly mgl = 0.039 N m of static torque for the payload alone. The arm's own mass, acceleration, friction and disturbances add load. A quoted stall torque is not a safe continuous operating point. Measure the actual mechanism and check the actuator's thermal and duty limits instead of buying a motor from a single headline number.

One small experiment every time

  1. Measure your wheel radius and track width, including uncertainty.
  2. Predict a slow straight run and a slow turn using the equations.
  3. Record wheel counts, time and an independent distance measurement.
  4. Repeat in both directions. A consistent offset suggests calibration; varying error suggests slip, timing or noise.
  5. Change exactly one parameter and repeat. Preserve the previous data so you can compare rather than remember.
Open the executable mathematical examples python
Save 10_control_math.py
"""Standard-library robotics calculations and a deliberately simple dynamic plant."""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import sin,cos,isfinite

def led_resistance(voltage:float,forward_drop:float,current_a:float)->float:
    if not all(map(isfinite,(voltage,forward_drop,current_a))) or current_a<=0 or voltage<=forward_drop:
        raise ValueError('Require finite supply > LED drop and positive current.')
    return (voltage-forward_drop)/current_a

def wheel_speeds(v:float,yaw_rate:float,radius:float,track:float):
    if radius<=0 or track<=0: raise ValueError('Radius and track must be positive.')
    return ((v-yaw_rate*track/2)/radius,(v+yaw_rate*track/2)/radius)

def forward_2link(l1:float,l2:float,q1:float,q2:float):
    if l1<=0 or l2<=0: raise ValueError('Link lengths must be positive.')
    return (l1*cos(q1)+l2*cos(q1+q2),l1*sin(q1)+l2*sin(q1+q2))

def stopping_distance(speed:float,delay_s:float,deceleration:float)->float:
    if speed<0 or delay_s<0 or deceleration<=0: raise ValueError('Invalid motion parameters.')
    return speed*delay_s+speed**2/(2*deceleration)

@dataclass
class PID:
    kp:float=1.5; ki:float=1.0; kd:float=0.0
    limit:float=3.0; integral:float=0.0; previous_error:float=0.0
    def update(self,target:float,measured:float,dt:float)->float:
        if dt<=0: raise ValueError('dt must be positive.')
        e=target-measured
        proposed=self.integral+e*dt
        raw=self.kp*e+self.ki*proposed+self.kd*(e-self.previous_error)/dt
        out=max(-self.limit,min(self.limit,raw))
        # Conditional integration prevents further windup into a saturated direction.
        if abs(raw)<self.limit or (raw>self.limit and e<0) or (raw<-self.limit and e>0):
            self.integral=proposed
        self.previous_error=e
        return out

def response(seconds=6.0,dt=0.01):
    controller=PID(); x=0.0; rows=[]
    for k in range(round(seconds/dt)):
        u=controller.update(1.0,x,dt)
        x += dt*((-x+u)/0.35) # First-order toy plant, not a specific real motor.
        rows.append(((k+1)*dt,x,u))
    return rows

if __name__=='__main__':
    import csv
    with open('pid_response.csv','w',newline='') as f:
        w=csv.writer(f); w.writerow(['time_s','measurement','command']); w.writerows(response())
    print('Wrote pid_response.csv; simulated toy plant, not hardware data.')

lessons.title: Feedback control: make motion predictable
lessons.intro: Use measured response, limits and latency instead of judging a controller by a smooth-looking animation.
lessons.body:
Imagine adjusting a shower. You feel the current temperature, compare it with your preference and change the tap. Delayed feedback makes it easy to overshoot. A motor controller has the same structure, but with measurable time, actuator limits and sensor noise. It should respond to what the mechanism actually did, not only what the application requested.

Read a PID controller as three different questions

error = target − measurement
command = Kp × error + Ki × accumulated error + Kd × error-change rate
TermPlain meaningFailure when used carelessly
P: proportionalHow far away am I now?Large gain can make the mechanism oscillate or saturate.
I: integralHave I been wrong in the same direction for a while?Stored error keeps demanding motion after a limit or obstruction.
D: derivativeHow quickly is the situation changing?Noise and target jumps can create large spikes.

The code uses a bounded integrator and a deliberately simple first-order plant. The graph below comes from executing that teaching model; it is not a measured SG90, a MuJoCo result or an industrial tuning recommendation. Real motion may require friction compensation, filtering, feedforward, cascaded loops and hardware-specific stability analysis.

Run the interactive version in the Sandbox, then record the result in your lab notebook.

Tune one property at a time

  1. Establish a safe low-speed operating envelope, disable large loads and verify the feedback sign.
  2. Record a small target step with zero integral action. Confirm positive error moves toward the target rather than away.
  3. Increase proportional gain cautiously. Observe rise time, overshoot and saturation, not only how fast the first movement looks.
  4. Add only enough integral action to address a measured steady bias. Clamp or back-calculate it when the actuator saturates.
  5. If derivative is useful, consider derivative on measured motion and an appropriate noise filter. Document the actual discrete-time equation.
  6. Change payload or friction and repeat the same experiment. One gain setting that works unloaded may fail with a heavier mechanism.
  7. Test command loss, sensor loss and startup. Control performance does not replace fault handling.

Timing creates physical distance

A rover moving at 0.30 m/s with 0.12 s perception-to-brake delay travels 0.036 m before deceleration begins. With constant achievable deceleration of 0.60 m/s squared, ideal braking adds 0.075 m. The illustrative total is 0.111 m before uncertainty or a safety margin. Real braking must be measured on the actual floor and load. This calculation is not a certified safe separation distance.

illustrative stopping distance = speed × delay + speed2 / (2 × deceleration)

Run the interactive version in the Sandbox, then record the result in your lab notebook.

What changes at the advanced level?

LQR designs a feedback law around a model and a chosen state/control cost. MPC repeatedly predicts a finite future and solves a constrained optimization problem. Neither is a magic replacement for sensor calibration or an inaccurate actuator model. Start by identifying the plant: apply a safe known input and measure how the real output responds. Keep a simple controller as the baseline against which complexity must earn its place.

lessons.title: Sensors disagree: calibration, uncertainty and state
lessons.intro: First verify signs, units, time and geometry. Then choose a filter that matches what can actually be observed.
lessons.body:
A robot does not observe its full physical state directly. An encoder measures rotation, a camera measures projected light and an IMU measures specific force and angular rate. Estimation combines imperfect evidence with a motion model. More sensors can make the system worse when their clocks, coordinate frames or calibration disagree.

Separate five errors before choosing a filter

ErrorExampleUseful experiment
BiasStationary gyro reads a small non-zero valueMeasure many stationary samples, at several temperatures if relevant.
ScaleWheel distance is always 6% too smallCompare multiple measured runs against an independent distance reference.
Axis/signTurning left is reported as rightRotate about one physical axis at a time and inspect the signed result.
TimingImage and pose are each correct but represent different momentsRecord acquisition timestamps and observe a controlled moving target.
Noise/outliersOccasional range spikes on a shiny targetPlot raw values with validity flags and repeat with different materials.

A Kalman update without mystery

Suppose your one-dimensional predicted position is 1.0 m with variance 0.04 m squared. An independent measurement says 1.2 m with variance 0.01 m squared. The gain P/(P+R) is 0.8. The corrected estimate is 1.0 + 0.8(1.2 - 1.0) = 1.16 m. This simple calculation trusts the lower-variance measurement more. It assumes the stated model, noise and independence are appropriate; a mislabelled or systematically wrong sensor is not repaired by the formula.

gain K = P / (P + R)
corrected state = predicted state + K × (measurement − predicted measurement)

An extended Kalman filter linearizes nonlinear functions locally. A factor graph instead represents relationships between states and observations in an optimization problem. Both need observability: the measurements must contain enough information to distinguish the state you are estimating. A six-axis IMU alone does not provide a stable absolute yaw reference indefinitely.

Local continuity and global correction are different

Wheel odometry should change smoothly over short intervals even while it slowly drifts. A map-based localization estimate may correct that accumulated drift. In ROS, the map-to-odom and odom-to-base_link structure separates these roles. Publishing competing transforms for the same parent-child relationship creates inconsistent evidence. Assign one clear owner to each transform.

Camera calibration that affects an actual task

  1. Fix the lens focus and choose the image resolution you will deploy.
  2. Acquire diverse, sharp calibration-target views spanning the image; nearly identical frontal frames are not enough.
  3. Estimate intrinsics and distortion, then inspect residuals and held-out target images.
  4. Determine the camera pose relative to the robot using a suitable extrinsic-calibration method.
  5. Move a target to known physical positions. Verify recovered geometry, not just a small training residual.
  6. Repeat the test after remounting the camera. Store calibration with the device and mounting revision.

Pixel coordinates are not millimetres. To turn a camera pixel into a 3D point you need the camera model and additional information such as depth, stereo geometry or a known plane. The red-object project intentionally reports pixel error only. That honesty is a strength: it avoids pretending a bounding-box centre is a safe grasp target.

lessons.title: Firmware and IoT that survive the real world
lessons.intro: Understand task scheduling, data ownership, command freshness, updates and recovery before adding a cloud dashboard.
lessons.body:
A tutorial assumes the cable stays connected and the program runs in the expected order. A product must also handle interrupted updates, slow storage, malformed commands, resets, brownouts and a device that reconnects after hours offline. The important design question is what physical state follows each failure.

A useful separation of responsibilities

LayerOwnsMust not depend on
Motor/actuator supervisionLimits, command age, local disable and fault latchingAn internet model returning on time.
Sensor acquisitionTimestamped readings, validity and calibration metadataA dashboard being open.
Behavior logicNamed states and explicit transitionsImplicit success inferred from a function call.
ConnectivityAuthentication, retries, telemetry queuesUnbounded RAM growth while disconnected.
User interfaceClear states and operator intentA misleading happy face while the mechanism is in fault.

C teaches storage, pointers and low-level device behavior. Modern C++ adds stronger abstractions such as RAII and explicit ownership when used carefully. Python is excellent for experiments, orchestration and perception, but ordinary Python on a general-purpose OS is not a hard real-time motor controller. Real-time means meeting deadlines reliably, not simply a small average latency.

Interrupts, tasks and shared data

An interrupt handles a time-sensitive event quickly and defers heavy work. A task can block, wait or process queued work under an RTOS scheduler. Shared memory needs an ownership or synchronization rule. volatile does not make a compound operation atomic and does not replace a mutex, queue or appropriate atomic primitive. Use a monotonic time source for elapsed-time decisions; wall-clock corrections should not extend a motor command's lifetime.

Specify a command as a contract

Inspect an illustrative command contract json
{
  "schema": "head_command.v1",
  "command_id": "example-00042",
  "mode": "bounded_position",
  "target_deg": 90,
  "valid_for_ms": 250,
  "device_id": "bench-head-01"
}

The receiver validates the schema, target range, authorized device/mode and command lifetime. A repeated command ID should not accidentally repeat a one-shot physical action. For network messages, use a deliberate freshness mechanism; a sender-provided timestamp without clock synchronization is not enough. An illustrative command limit is not a universal safe servo range.

MQTT does not make commands exactly-once physical actions

Delivery semantics describe message delivery, not the physical effect of application code. A reconnect can expose a retained command or replay a message. Prefer explicit command IDs, expiry and acknowledgements for state changes. Telemetry can tolerate a different policy than motion requests. Keep broker credentials out of source control; authorize each device narrowly. Never let an arbitrary topic string become an arbitrary shell command.

A firmware release has a recovery path

  1. Record the exact toolchain, library versions, board revision and configuration.
  2. Run unit tests for parsers and state transitions on the host; then run device-level tests for timing and peripherals.
  3. Build a versioned image and verify its origin/integrity through an appropriate signed-update design.
  4. Test interrupted download and interrupted activation. Retain a known-good recovery path.
  5. Boot the new firmware into a bounded self-test/confirmation sequence rather than immediately enabling all actuators.
  6. Record which version each device actually runs. Practice rollback on a bench device before a customer needs it.
