lessons.title: Robot learning: data, actions and evidence
lessons.intro: Learn a complete experimental method rather than treating RL training as a Play button.
lessons.body:
There are three separate tasks hidden in the phrase "teach a robot." You must define what observations are available, what actions the mechanism can execute and what counts as success. A language model may interpret "put the red block in the tray," but it does not automatically provide a calibrated camera, a valid collision-free path or a stable gripper controller.

MethodWhat the learning signal isA sensible first comparison
Behavior cloningDemonstrated observation-action pairsA repeatable hand-programmed motion on the same narrow task.
Reinforcement learningRewards from environment interactionA conventional controller on a task with measurable dynamics.
Diffusion/flow-based action policiesA learned distribution over action sequencesA simpler imitation policy with the same training/evaluation data.
Vision-language-action modelVisual/state/language context mapped to actionsTask-specific policy plus separately verified instruction parsing.
High-level LLM plannerStructured goals, tools and observationsA small deterministic task/state machine.

A reward is a specification that can be exploited

Suppose a robot is rewarded for being close to a box. It may remain near the box without grasping it. Rewarding a gripper-close command does not prove contact. Define success through a task-relevant observation: the correct object is in the target area and remains there after release. Penalize unsafe events separately and keep independent constraints outside the reward where appropriate. The tiny grid project deliberately makes this distinction visible before you spend GPU time.

A reproducible learning experiment

  1. Write the task, observation schema, action units/limits, reset distribution and termination conditions before training.
  2. Create a simple baseline. If it fails because the sensor is wrong, repair the sensor instead of increasing model size.
  3. Separate training, validation and final test episodes by the source of correlation: session, object, scene or operator, not just random adjacent frames.
  4. Log seeds, dataset hashes, calibration revision, software version, reward components and compute budget.
  5. Inspect learning curves and actual rollouts. A scalar reward can hide collisions or repeated resets.
  6. Evaluate without exploration noise on held-out conditions. Report success, interventions, cycle time and failure categories, not only the best clip.
  7. Deploy gradually behind a bounded action interface, with independent stopping and recovery behavior.

Action chunks create a timing problem

Predicting a short sequence of future actions can reduce inference overhead. But when the world changes, the remaining actions may refer to stale observations. Measure the age of the observation at execution, not just the inference duration. An asynchronous pipeline needs clear rules for cancellation, overlapping chunks, queue depth and operator stop. A faster benchmark is not proof that every task becomes safer or more reactive.

Read foundation-model papers without surrendering judgment

SmolVLA and GR00T N1 are useful research case studies for language-conditioned robot behavior and data/model design. They are cited here as specific published work, not as the latest model ranking or as drop-in solutions for any robot. Read the embodiment, action representation, training-data distribution, deployment requirements and evaluation protocol. A model trained around one joint/state interface cannot simply be connected to an unrelated actuator bus.

For your background as an AI engineer, a strong specialization is the bridge between models and physical evidence: dataset quality, evaluation, latency-aware execution, failure recovery and sim-to-real testing. These remain valuable even when a particular model architecture changes.

lessons.title: Why a beautiful digital twin can still be wrong
lessons.intro: Treat simulation as a falsifiable model and progressively earn the right to deploy more energetic behavior.
lessons.body:
A simulator is a model of a physical system. It is useful when it preserves the properties that matter for the decision you are making. A photorealistic wall does not repair incorrect wheel friction. A carefully fitted motor model does not make a synthetic camera image reproduce every reflection. Validate each layer against a measurable real-world reference.

Use a discrepancy log

LayerMismatch to look forPractical evidence
GeometryWrong link origin, wheel radius or collision proxyMeasured dimensions and controlled pose comparison.
Mass/inertiaIncorrect weight distributionMeasured mass and response to safe motion experiments.
ActuationDelay, deadband, saturation, backlashCommand/encoder/current recordings at small safe inputs.
ContactSlipping, restitution, complianceRepeated ramps, turns or drops with controlled surfaces.
SensingBias, noise, latency, occlusionTimestamped sensor logs against an independent reference.
BehaviorController reset or recovery differsThe same fault scenarios executed in both environments.

Domain randomization varies uncertain quantities during training. It is most meaningful when the ranges reflect real variation rather than arbitrary numbers. System identification estimates model parameters from measured behavior. Use both: identify what you can, randomize what remains uncertain, then test transfer. Keep the physical robot's action limits independent of the trained policy.

The simulation-to-bench release ladder

  1. Validate model geometry and passive motion before enabling a learned controller.
  2. Compare an easy conventional controller across simulation and hardware. This exposes basic interface mismatches.
  3. Replay observations offline through the candidate policy with outputs logged but not applied.
  4. Run low-energy, mechanically constrained bench tests with an independent stop path.
  5. Expand speed, payload and workspace only after the preceding conditions have measured acceptable outcomes.
  6. Introduce known disturbances and faults under controlled conditions.
  7. Repeat on different days and with changed conditions. A single successful transfer does not establish broad reliability.

What a safety argument is trying to show

List hazards, initiating conditions, prevention/detection measures and residual risk. A hobby test rig is not an industrial safety system. Software emergency-stop buttons, ordinary network commands and an AI safety prompt are not interchangeable with a properly designed independent protective function. Requirements depend on product and jurisdiction; have qualified specialists assess applicable electrical, machine, radio and product requirements before commercialization.

Physical boundary. These labs are low-energy learning exercises. They are not instructions to qualify a collaborative industrial robot or operate an unguarded machine near people.

lessons.intro: Separate unit evidence, integration evidence, simulated evidence and measured physical evidence.
lessons.body:
A senior engineer asks what evidence would disprove the design. Testing should cover the mechanism, firmware, data interfaces and operator workflow. A passing Python test cannot prove a motor driver is wired correctly. A successful video cannot prove the system handles corrupted commands. Use different tests for different claims.

Test layerExampleWhat passing means
UnitReject a negative command lifetimeThat function handles the tested inputs.
IntegrationSensor frame reaches the correct ROS consumerThe tested components agree on interfaces.
Software-in-loopPlanner handles a blocked simulated aisleThe modeled scenario passes.
Hardware-in-loopController output is measured against a safe test loadSelected real electrical/timing behavior matches the test.
Physical taskRover stops before a marked line in repeated conditionsMeasured system behavior in those conditions, not all possible conditions.
Operator/pilotAnother person assembles, starts and recovers itInstructions and workflow work for that trial.

A small fault-injection plan

Fault to introduce safelyDesired behaviorEvidence to save
Camera stops producing framesTarget state becomes stale; downstream motion does not continue indefinitelyFrame age, state transition and command log.
Sensor disconnectINVALID / fault, not a plausible zeroDisconnect time and reported validity.
Network outageLocal bounded behavior and controlled reconnectCommand expiry and reconnect events.
Duplicate commandNo unintended repeat of a one-shot actionCommand ID and acknowledgement history.
Time-source adjustmentMonotonic expiry still worksTiming-source choice and elapsed-time trace.
Application crashIndependent actuator supervisor reaches the specified safe stateExternal observation of disable latency.
Update interruptionDevice recovers into a known-good image or recovery modeBoot/update logs and version evidence.

Latency is a distribution

Track acquisition time, transport/queueing, inference, planning, actuation dispatch and physical response. Report p50, p95, p99 and worst observed under a stated workload, not only an average on an idle computer. Also report the number of samples. A process that is fast 99 times and freezes once can be unacceptable for a physical control deadline.

Statistics: what ten good demos do not prove

If failures were independent and the true failure probability were 10%, the chance of seeing zero failures in ten trials would still be 0.9 to the power 10, about 35%. Ten clean demonstrations therefore do not establish a very small failure rate. Real repeated trials may be correlated, making naive counting even weaker. Vary conditions deliberately and distinguish exploratory testing from a prespecified qualification plan.

lessons.title: From a prototype to a product people can maintain
lessons.intro: Engineer the installation, service and economics alongside the machine itself.
lessons.body:
A company is not a larger demo. It must solve a repeated customer problem while covering manufacturing, installation, support, repair and failure costs. Begin with a narrow workflow and a measurable baseline. A less glamorous mechanism with predictable uptime can be a better product than a general-purpose robot that needs constant supervision.

Write the problem before selecting a robot

Example discovery exercise: a workshop spends time checking whether a part is present in a tray. First observe the actual process. Can a simple presence sensor, fixture change or camera solve the problem without an arm? Ask who owns the result, what a missed detection costs, how products vary and who maintains the station. Do not equate an enthusiastic conversation with a paid commitment.

Build a cost model with honest boundaries

Cost categoryQuestions to answer
Purchased componentsExact part, supplier, alternatives, minimum quantity and shipping?
ManufacturingPrint/PCB yield, failed parts, labour, fixture and rework time?
InstallationWho mounts, calibrates, trains the operator and documents acceptance?
OperationPower, connectivity, compute, consumables and periodic calibration?
SupportRemote diagnosis, travel, spare units, returns and warranty reserve?
Commercial responsibilityApplicable compliance assessment, insurance, privacy, licences and contracts?

Illustrative arithmetic, not a market quote. If a device sells for 20,000 currency units and all variable delivery/support costs total 12,000, contribution before fixed overhead is 8,000. Calling the 8,000 net profit would omit salaries, development, compliance and other fixed costs. A low bill of materials alone does not establish a viable business.

Make the build reproducible

  1. Freeze a prototype revision: CAD, circuit, firmware, configuration and calibration are versioned together.
  2. Prepare a photo-based assembly traveller. Each step names the part, fastener, orientation, tool and inspection.
  3. Add a power-off continuity check and a current-limited first-power procedure appropriate to the design.
  4. Use a test fixture or repeatable method to verify each unit. Record serial number and test results.
  5. Define replaceable modules and connector access. Practise disassembly without damaging cables or adhesives.
  6. Write operator start/stop, recovery and cleaning instructions. Test them with someone who did not design the robot.
  7. Run a bounded customer pilot with agreed success measures and explicit support ownership.
  8. Investigate every intervention. Improve the workflow before scaling the fleet.

A photo brief for your own commercial manual

Required shotWhat to showWhy a stock picture is insufficient
Front / rear / top / undersideExact assembled revision and scale referencePorts and mountings vary between revisions.
Enclosure openActual cable routes, fasteners and strain reliefA rendered cutaway can hide interference.
Assembly stagesEach intermediate state before it becomes hiddenA final photograph cannot explain order.
Connector close-upsReadable pin labels and locking featuresColour alone is not a wiring contract.
Operating sequenceNormal, warning, fault and recovery statesA promotional image proves none of these.

The reference assembly photographs in this book teach how to inspect a build. They are not photographs of a custom MIRA or Desk Buddy that has been assembled and qualified. Capture your own revision-specific evidence before presenting an original product as build-ready.

lessons.title: Future-facing research without invented certainty
lessons.intro: Develop research judgment by identifying uncertainty and designing a decisive experiment.
lessons.body:
There is no reliable way to promise a secret technology that nobody else knows and that will certainly create a company. A more useful research habit is to find a recurring failure in current systems, form a testable hypothesis and measure whether a proposed solution changes the outcome. The following are research directions, not guaranteed market forecasts.

DirectionA concrete beginner-to-research experimentWhat could invalidate the idea
Failure-aware robot learningLabel failed attempts and test whether a recovery classifier reduces human interventions.The extra detector produces too many false stops or fails on new scenes.
Latency-aware action executionCompare synchronous and bounded asynchronous policy execution under injected delay.Throughput improves while stale-action hazards increase.
Contact-aware manipulationCompare vision-only grasp verification with an added force/current/tactile cue.The extra sensor is noisy, fragile or costly to calibrate.
Data quality and calibration lineageTrain on the same number of episodes with versus without calibrated, well-timed observations.The apparent gain comes from an easier train/test split.
Sim-to-real model validationIdentify actuator delay and friction, then measure transfer before/after updating the model.An improvement on one surface overfits and harms another.
Serviceable low-cost robotsMeasure repair time and failure rate for modular versus tightly packed assemblies.Extra connectors introduce more failures than the modularity saves.

A one-page research protocol

  1. State one falsifiable hypothesis, not a product slogan.
  2. List the baseline and exactly what changes in the proposed method.
  3. Declare the task distribution and the success/failure/intervention metrics.
  4. Choose the evaluation split before looking at the final test data.
  5. Run repeated trials and preserve unsuccessful ones.
  6. Report uncertainty, compute cost, hardware configuration and practical limitations.
  7. Ask another person to reproduce one result from your instructions.

SmolVLA is one published example of exploring compact language-conditioned policies and asynchronous execution. GR00T N1 is one published foundation-model case study. The lasting learning objective is to understand observation/action interfaces, data provenance and evaluation, not to memorize a product name or assume it is the latest release.

lessons.title: Senior interview studio: reason from evidence
lessons.intro: Practise eighteen realistic design and debugging conversations with sample reasoning and evidence requirements.
lessons.body:
Use these as oral design exercises, not memorized scripts. Answer in four stages: clarify the system, state the failure/risk, propose a measured diagnosis and define evidence that would change your mind. The sample responses are starting points; a real interviewer may deliberately change the assumptions.

01. The ESP32 resets only when a servo starts. What do you do?

Suspect a power transient before an AI or timing bug. Reproduce at a bounded load, inspect supply voltage at the board during motion, check common reference and the separate actuator power path, inspect stall/load conditions, and compare against a known adequate supply. Preserve the reset reason. Do not hide the symptom by disabling brownout protection.

Evidence to bring: Power trace, current/load condition, reset log and a repeatable before/after test.

02. Your motor turns away from the target. Retune PID?

First disable or limit actuation and verify command sign, encoder sign, joint axis and units. A wrong feedback sign creates positive feedback. Only tune after a small safe command demonstrably moves the measurement toward the target.

Evidence to bring: A sign-and-units table and a low-energy motion trace.

03. The robot is perfect in RViz but falls in Gazebo.

RViz visualizes geometry and data; it does not validate mass, contact or dynamics. Inspect collision shapes, link origins, joint axes, inertias, gravity and controller activation. Test passive dynamics before control.

Evidence to bring: A minimal model that reproduces the fall, not a screenshot alone.

04. A ROS publisher and subscriber appear healthy but no messages arrive.

Check topic names, types, domain/network discovery, QoS compatibility, namespace/remapping and callback execution. Observe each end with ROS inspection tools. Do not start by changing every QoS setting at once.

Evidence to bring: Node/topic inspection, actual QoS policies and a minimal compatible pair.

05. How do you choose a sensor frequency?

Derive it from motion dynamics, allowed state age, observability and end-to-end latency. Check bandwidth, processing load, anti-aliasing and worst-case queueing. A higher publication rate with stale queued frames can be worse than a lower rate with fresh data.

Evidence to bring: A timing budget and stale-data tests under load.

06. Why is the point cloud rotated 90 degrees?

Inspect camera optical-axis convention, extrinsic transform, parent frame and quaternion/rotation composition. Validate one known physical direction and timestamp. Avoid changing the renderer to mask an underlying geometry error.

Evidence to bring: An axis drawing and a recorded calibration check.

07. The learned policy has higher reward but lower task success.

Disaggregate reward components and inspect rollouts. Check reward hacking, termination/reset behavior, success definition and evaluation distribution. Evaluate the task independently of the training reward and compare interventions and constraint violations.

Evidence to bring: Held-out evaluation with videos, numerical traces and failure labels.

08. When should an autonomous agent stop?

Use explicit success evidence, deadline/action budget, resource/energy bounds, stale or invalid observations, safety constraints and recovery limits. Planning stop and physical stop are different: the execution layer must reach the defined bounded state independently of the planner.

Evidence to bring: A state machine with termination reasons and fault-injection tests.

09. How do you collect demonstrations efficiently?

Standardize the task, camera mounting, calibration and episode metadata. Start with clean diverse successful demonstrations, retain useful failure labels, avoid redundant near-identical episodes and test coverage gaps. Record operator interventions rather than hiding them.

Evidence to bring: Dataset schema, calibration revision and an evaluation split by session/scene.

10. Why not call a cloud LLM for every motor command?

Network and inference latency are variable and the model does not provide a deterministic low-level safety guarantee. Use it for bounded high-level interpretation/planning; local execution checks freshness, limits, state and stop conditions.

Evidence to bring: A layered control architecture and behavior under lost connectivity.

11. How do you know a simulator is good enough?

Good enough is task-specific. Compare geometry, actuator response, sensing/timing and relevant contact behavior against independent real measurements. Quantify the discrepancy that matters to the intended decision.

Evidence to bring: A model-validation matrix and transfer results with limitations.

12. How should a robot recover after losing localization?

Enter a defined bounded state based on the environment and risk, report uncertainty, prevent ungrounded navigation and attempt only an explicitly allowed recovery. Do not silently reset the pose to a convenient value and continue.

Evidence to bring: A localization-loss scenario and its observed state transitions.

13. A 99% average success rate is reported. Is that enough?

Ask for trial count, confidence/uncertainty, task distribution, failure severity, interventions and correlated conditions. A small failure rate with high consequence can still be unacceptable; average performance may hide a fragile subgroup.

Evidence to bring: Raw trial outcomes and condition-stratified metrics.

14. How would you deploy new firmware to 100 devices?

Stage rollout by hardware/software compatibility, authenticate updates, preserve recovery and rollback, verify boot health and observe per-device state. Test interruptions and avoid enabling actuation before the required checks pass.

Evidence to bring: A rollout state machine, signed artifact identity and a rollback demonstration.

15. Why can reliable middleware be wrong for camera data?

Reliable delivery may be suitable, but queueing/retransmission can make old frames arrive late. Choose policies from freshness, loss tolerance and bandwidth requirements. Compatibility and bounded queue depth are part of the design, not a universal reliable-versus-best-effort rule.

Evidence to bring: Latency/age distributions under congestion for the chosen QoS.

16. Your code passes tests. Why does the assembled unit fail?

Unit tests do not cover all physical connections, timing, mounting, power and environmental conditions. Classify the failure layer, collect evidence and reproduce it with the smallest safe setup. Expand the right test layer after the fix.

Evidence to bring: A root-cause record and a new regression test at the appropriate layer.

17. How do you reduce robotics product cost?

First measure where cost comes from: parts, assembly time, failures, service and downtime. Simplify the task/mechanism where possible. Check that a cheaper component does not increase calibration, support or failure costs.

Evidence to bring: A lifecycle cost comparison rather than BOM price alone.

18. What would you learn first for a senior role?

Choose a role-specific depth: embedded control, autonomy, manipulation, perception or robot learning. Build enough breadth to explain interfaces and own one end-to-end result. Use measured projects to demonstrate design tradeoffs, debugging and delivery rather than a long list of framework names.

Evidence to bring: A reproducible repository, test report, assembly/operation guide and technical defence.

A fair self-assessment

Integration competenceYou can diagnose time, frame, units, data validity and power problems across components.
Autonomy competenceYou can reproduce a simulated navigation/manipulation workflow and explain its failure modes.
Robot-learning competenceYou can defend data splits, action interfaces, evaluation and deployment boundaries.
Senior ownershipYou lead a bounded subsystem/product outcome, quantify reliability, document tradeoffs and support recovery.

lessons.title: Learn it, build it, then teach it
lessons.intro: Move through evidence-based milestones and turn each build into a teachable, reproducible lesson.
lessons.body:
You already have software/AI experience, so you need not repeat every beginner programming exercise. The areas that deserve patience are electrical power, mechanics, measurement, timing, control and physical failure. Advance when you can show the evidence below, not simply when a number of weeks has passed.

StageRead / operateBuildExit evidence
RecognizeWorkbench, component atlases, board anatomyProjects 1-5Identify actual pins/components and explain invalid readings.
IntegrateWires, firmware, mechanicsProjects 6-12A repeatable assembly, power budget, state machine and fault log.
SimulateVersion setup and platform toursProjects 13-16A clean launch, known model parameters, plots and reproducible reset.
LearnControl, estimation and robot learningProjects 17-19Baseline, data split, trained/evaluated policy and recorded limits.
DeliverTesting, product and interview studioProject 20Someone else can assemble/run/recover the bounded system.

A productive two-hour practice session

  1. Spend the first 15 minutes predicting one result on paper.
  2. Spend 45 minutes running the smallest safe experiment.
  3. Spend 20 minutes comparing expected and actual behavior.
  4. Spend 20 minutes writing a labelled photo, plot or short explanation.
  5. Use the final 20 minutes to reproduce the result from a clean start or explain it to another learner.

This is a suggested study structure, not a promise of how quickly expertise appears. Some faults deserve several sessions. Record what did not work: a well-explained failed experiment is more valuable than an unexplained polished animation.

Teach a beginner without hiding the hard part

Show the actual part first. Ask the learner to point to the connector, power input and signal. Explain one physical idea, predict a result and run a small test. Deliberately introduce one safe fault, such as a disconnected unpowered signal wire, and teach diagnosis. Do not ask a beginner to paste a large unknown program and call that understanding.

lessons.intro: Fifty-three engineering terms connected to the physical system rather than left as buzzwords.
lessons.body:

TermMeaning

ActuatorA component that changes the physical world, such as a motor or solenoid.
BacklashLost motion when mechanical clearance is taken up after reversing direction.
Baud rateSymbol rate on a communication link; both ends must use compatible settings.
BOMBill of materials: exact parts and quantities for one product revision.

CalibrationRelating measurements or geometry to a known reference.

DeadlineThe latest permitted completion time, not an average performance goal.

lessons.title: Start with a question, not a shopping list
lessons.intro: Turn curiosity into a small experiment you can actually finish.
lessons.body:
The robot is not the problem

A robot is a solution candidate. First describe a job: move a light object between two fixed trays, inspect a printed label, or remind a worker without moving. State the environment, the acceptable error and what failure costs. A stationary camera may solve the job better than a walking robot.

Predict, change, measure, explain

Before each lab, write one prediction. Change one variable. Measure the result, including a failure. Then explain why the prediction agreed or disagreed. For an LED experiment, predict what happens to current when resistance doubles while voltage is unchanged. This makes the equation meaningful.

Your first evidence package

Keep four items together: the question, the exact configuration, the raw measurements and the conclusion. Record software versions and hardware revision. A screenshot with no settings is difficult to reproduce. A video is useful, but it does not replace a timestamped experiment record.

A first-session challenge

Open the circuit sandbox. Use 3.3 V, a 2 V LED and 220 ohms. Predict 5.91 mA. Change to 440 ohms and expect about 2.95 mA. This simplified model ignores LED nonlinearities and GPIO output resistance; name those assumptions in your notebook.

quizzes.question: Which result is most useful to another engineer?
options: A prediction, setup, data and explanation
quizzes.explanation: Reproducible evidence lets another person test your conclusion.

lessons.title: Numbers become position, speed and force
lessons.intro: Learn the mathematics in the order your robot needs it.
lessons.body:
Units are part of a number

A wheel radius of 30 means nothing until you state millimetres or metres. Convert 30 mm to 0.030 m before using SI equations. Angles in most programming-library trigonometric functions are radians: 180 degrees equals pi radians. A unit mistake can look like a control bug.

A derivative is a local rate

If an encoder position changes from 1.00 rad to 1.05 rad in 0.01 s, the average angular speed is 5 rad/s. A numerical derivative uses differences over a time interval. Smaller intervals do not automatically improve it: position noise is divided by that interval too.

An integral is accumulation

Travel at 0.2 m/s for 3 seconds and distance is 0.6 m. For varying speed, sum speed times each sample interval. Bias also accumulates: a false 0.01 m/s for 100 seconds creates a 1 m position error. This is why dead reckoning needs external correction.

Vectors, matrices and frames

The vector [2,1] may describe a target in the robot frame or the room frame. Those are different facts. A rotation matrix changes coordinates without changing the physical point. For a 90 degree planar rotation, [x,y] becomes [-y,x]. Test [1,0] to obtain [0,1].

Practice gate

Implement degrees-to-radians, a 2D rotation and a finite-difference velocity in the Code view. Test zero, negative angles and a full revolution. Then explain why the magnitude of a rotated vector should remain unchanged.

quizzes.question: Why can differentiating encoder measurements amplify noise?
options: Noise is multiplied by the wheel radius only
The position difference is divided by a small time interval
quizzes.explanation: A small noisy difference divided by a small dt can become a large apparent velocity.

lessons.title: Voltage, current and components as a system
lessons.intro: Move from memorizing pin names to explaining an electrical path.
lessons.body:
A complete path

Current needs a closed path. Voltage is a difference between two points, not a substance flowing in a wire. A resistor limits current according to a simple model; an LED is directional and nonlinear. Ground is the reference node, not a magical sink for unwanted electricity.

Series and parallel

Series resistors carry the same current and their resistances add. Parallel branches share voltage; their currents add at the junction. Two 1 kilohm resistors in parallel have 500 ohms equivalent resistance. A GPIO is not an ideal power supply: its drive capability and voltage limits matter.

Dividers and loading

A 10 kilohm upper resistor and a 20 kilohm lower resistor give 5 V times 20/(10+20), or 3.33 V, only for an unloaded ideal divider. Connecting a low-resistance load changes the ratio. A divider suitable for a signal is not a regulator for a motor.

Capacitors and time

A capacitor stores charge. The RC time constant is resistance times capacitance. With 10 kilohms and 10 microfarads, tau is 0.1 s. After one tau, ideal charging reaches about 63 percent of the final value. Supply decoupling and low-pass filtering use this behavior.

Safe measurement

For resistance or continuity, disconnect power. Measure voltage in parallel with the points of interest. Current measurement requires a suitable series connection and meter input; placing a current-range meter across a supply can short it. For beginner labs, stay with protected, low-voltage supplies.

quizzes.question: Can a resistive voltage divider be used as a general motor power supply?
options: Yes, if the output voltage looks correct unloaded
No; loading changes the divider and power requirements matter
Only when the resistor colors match
quizzes.explanation: Voltage, current capacity and power dissipation must all be designed.

lessons.title: From a variable to a reliable control loop
lessons.intro: Python for reasoning; C and C++ for hardware and systems work.
lessons.body:
State has a lifetime

A variable stores information. A state machine gives that information meaning: IDLE, LISTENING, THINKING and SPEAKING. A transition should depend on a defined event, such as a button edge or an audio-complete signal, not on a guessed delay.

Types and memory

A signed integer can represent negative numbers; an unsigned one cannot. In C and C++, fixed-width types make intent clearer, but overflow and conversions still require care. A pointer is an address, not the object itself. Never return an address to a local stack object after its lifetime ends.

Functions and interfaces

Separate reading a sensor, validating the sample and choosing an action. Return a value plus validity and timestamp instead of silently returning zero on failure. Zero metres could mean collision; it must not also secretly mean a disconnected sensor.

Blocking versus cooperative work

delay(1000) prevents the simple foreground loop from doing other work for that period. A nonblocking schedule checks elapsed time and lets other tasks run. An RTOS adds scheduling tools, but it does not repair race conditions or an overloaded processor by itself.

A small test first

Write a function that clamps a requested motor command to its permitted range. Test below minimum, exactly at the limits, above maximum and non-finite input. Define what failure does: for an actuator command, reject invalid values and request the safe state.

quizzes.question: A sensor failed. Which interface is clearest?
options: Return 0 and hope the caller knows
Return value, validity and measurement time
Reuse the last number forever without marking it
quizzes.explanation: Validity and freshness are part of the measurement contract.

lessons.title: Loads, torque and why plastic parts fail
lessons.intro: Learn mechanics before adding stronger motors.
lessons.body:
Force and leverage

Holding a 0.2 kg object 0.1 m from a horizontal joint requires about 0.2 times 9.81 times 0.1 = 0.196 Nm, before counting the arm itself. Acceleration, friction and uncertainty increase the required margin. Published stall torque is not a safe continuous operating torque.

Stiffness, strength and backlash

A part can survive without being stiff enough. Flex makes the gripper miss its target. Backlash is lost motion when direction reverses; increasing controller gain cannot remove mechanical clearance. Measure both deflection under load and repeatability from opposite directions.

Bearings and fasteners

Use bearings to support loads rather than expecting a small servo output shaft to carry every bending load. Fasteners need access for tools. A screw driven repeatedly into printed plastic may wear the hole; inserts or captive nuts can improve serviceability.

Design around real parts

Measure the actual board, connector and cable bend radius. Add mounting clearances based on your printer and fit test, not a universal allowance. Print a small gauge before a full enclosure. Keep the radio antenna away from shielding metal and noisy cable bundles.

Manufacturing exercise

For a desk robot, sketch three separate systems: the enclosure, the load path and the wiring harness. Mark how the lid opens, where strain relief sits and which parts must be removed to replace a failed servo. A beautiful sealed shell can be an expensive maintenance mistake.

quizzes.question: Why is stall torque not a suitable continuous design target?
options: Stall is always the most efficient condition
Heating, current and duty cycle can make it unsustainable
quizzes.explanation: Continuous operation must respect thermal and electrical limits, not just a maximum stalled value.

lessons.title: Noise is not the same as being wrong
lessons.intro: Learn uncertainty before trusting a sensor-fusion output.
lessons.body:
Three different errors

Noise varies between readings. Bias shifts readings in a consistent direction. Outliers are unusual large errors. Averaging can reduce some independent zero-mean noise, but it cannot automatically remove a fixed bias or repair a damaged sensor.

Mean, spread and evidence

Measure a stationary target 100 times. Compute the mean and standard deviation, then compare the mean with a known distance. Record missing readings too. Reporting only the cleanest ten readings hides the operational failure rate.

Combining information

Suppose two independent unbiased distance estimates have standard deviations 1 cm and 2 cm. Weighting by inverse variance gives the first estimate four times the weight. Independence matters: two algorithms using the same faulty camera can agree and still be wrong.

Bayesian reasoning

A prior represents what you believe before a new measurement. The likelihood describes how plausible that measurement is for different states. The posterior combines them. A Kalman filter uses a structured model of this process under specific assumptions; the output is an estimate, not proof.

Practice gate

Create a noisy constant signal in code and compare its raw data, moving average and a deliberately biased version. Plot error against the known truth, not just how smooth the line looks. Explain the delay introduced by a longer smoothing window.

quizzes.question: What does averaging fail to remove by itself?
quizzes.explanation: A biased sensor can become very consistently wrong after averaging.

lessons.title: Your robotics workstation is a reproducible experiment
lessons.intro: Understand files, processes and environments before stacking packages.
lessons.body:
A terminal is a control surface

The current directory affects relative paths. A process has a working directory, environment variables and an exit code. Keep project code in Git, store raw experiments separately, and do not use sudo as a universal fix for permissions errors.

Isolate dependencies

Use a Python virtual environment for each non-ROS Python project. ROS packages belong to compatible workspaces and distributions. Record your OS, compiler and package versions. A random mixture of two distributions can create failures that resemble algorithm bugs.

Read a failure from the boundary inward

Check power and cable, then device discovery, permissions, transport, protocol and application behavior. For a ROS sensor, inspect the publisher, topic type, QoS and frame/timestamp before changing visualization settings.

Reproduction exercise

Make a README that starts from a clean shell, creates the environment, installs a pinned set of dependencies, runs one command and identifies the expected result. Ask another person to run it without verbal hints. Record every missing assumption as a documentation defect.

quizzes.question: A Python import fails. What should you check first?
quizzes.explanation: The interpreter may not be the one into which the dependency was installed.

lessons.title: Sampling, aliasing and the age of a measurement
lessons.intro: Timing is part of correctness, not just a performance statistic.
lessons.body:
Sampling changes what you can see

If you sample a rotating wheel too slowly, it can appear to rotate backwards. Sampling requires a model of signal bandwidth and an appropriate anti-alias filter. A higher update rate is useful only when the measurement itself supports it.

Timestamp where the event happened

The measurement time is not necessarily the time a network message arrives. Store the acquisition timestamp and a sequence number. Synchronize clocks or estimate their offsets when combining devices. Delay can make two correct individual measurements describe different physical moments.

Jitter and deadlines

Latency is elapsed time. Jitter is variation in timing. A periodic controller may tolerate a bounded delay but fail with occasional very long gaps. Measure distributions and worst observed behavior under realistic load rather than just reporting an average.

A concrete budget

At 0.5 m/s, a 100 ms reaction delay adds 0.05 m of travel before braking begins. With ideal constant deceleration 1 m/s squared, braking adds v squared divided by 2a = 0.125 m. The ideal total is 0.175 m; a real system needs margins for traction, sensing and faults.

Lab

Run the rover sandbox and compare a low command rate with a smoother rate in your own exported simulation. Log the timestep. For hardware, use a logic analyzer or timestamped GPIO trace to measure execution intervals. Do not call a browser animation hard real time.

quizzes.question: A robot travels 0.5 m/s during 0.1 s of reaction delay. How far does it travel before braking?
quizzes.explanation: Distance during delay equals speed times delay.

lessons.title: A pixel is a direction, not a distance
lessons.intro: Learn what a camera can and cannot measure.
lessons.body:
Image coordinates

A pixel location tells you where something projects on an image. Without a depth source or known geometry, one pixel does not uniquely identify a 3D point. A small nearby object and a large distant object may occupy the same image area.

Intrinsic and extrinsic calibration

Intrinsics model focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Extrinsics locate the camera relative to another coordinate frame. A correctly calibrated camera can still fail if you apply a transform in the wrong direction or mix optical and robot axis conventions.

The pinhole approximation

With focal length fx in pixels, a point with camera coordinates X and Z projects to u = fx times X/Z + cx. With fx=600, X=0.1 m, Z=1 m and cx=320, u=380 pixels. This ideal example omits distortion.

Verification before neural networks

Record a calibration target from different angles. Reserve some views for evaluation. Inspect reprojection errors and test the geometry at a new position. A detector confidence score is not a calibrated probability that a grasp is safe.

Practice gate

Use the color-tracking project to find a centroid, then deliberately vary lighting and add a distractor. Define a lost-target state and reject tiny detections. Only after that should you convert image error to an appropriately limited command.

quizzes.question: Does one 2D pixel identify a unique 3D location?
options: No, depth or additional geometry is needed
Only if the camera is expensive
quizzes.explanation: A pixel corresponds to a viewing direction; distance remains ambiguous.

lessons.title: How to tell whether a robot policy learned anything useful
lessons.intro: Evaluate outcomes, failures and distribution shift.
lessons.body:
Define success before training

Write a rule a stranger could use to score a trial. For a pick-and-place task, specify object, start region, target tolerance, maximum duration and whether human intervention counts as failure. Then define safety violations separately from success.

Separate training from evaluation

Keep evaluation episodes, object placements or sessions out of training. Frame-level random splits can leak nearly identical images between sets. Split by episode or collection session where appropriate. Keep a simple classical baseline.

Use more than a reward curve

Reward can rise because the policy exploits a loophole. Record completion rate, collisions, interventions, time and performance after changes in lighting, payload or friction. Repeat across seeds and preserve failed episodes.

Small samples are weak evidence

Nine successes out of ten is an observation, not proof of 90 percent reliability everywhere. State the sample size and test conditions. A binomial confidence interval or Bayesian interval can communicate uncertainty better than a single percentage.

Practice here

In the Q-learning sandbox, train a policy and then evaluate it from multiple nonterminal starting cells. Compare greedy-policy success with a random-policy baseline. This tiny deterministic grid demonstrates the procedure; it is not evidence of real robot manipulation capability.

quizzes.question: Which split best avoids adjacent-frame leakage?
options: Split complete episodes or recording sessions
quizzes.explanation: Adjacent frames can be nearly duplicates. Episode-level separation is a stronger start.

lessons.title: From ROS demo to industrial cell
lessons.intro: Learn the boundary between useful software and a qualified machine.
lessons.body:
Different responsibilities

A planner proposes motion. A controller tracks it. Independent safety functions enforce appropriate protective behavior. A ROS node, an ordinary GPIO button or a language model must not be advertised as a certified safety system merely because it can stop a demo.

Integration contracts

Define units, coordinate frames, message types, timeouts, heartbeat behavior and authority to command motion. Consider how a PLC, fieldbus, robot controller and ROS application interact. Restart and partial-communication failures are normal test cases, not rare curiosities.

Commissioning sequence

Validate geometry without motor power where possible. Check joint signs, limits and calibration. Use reduced speed and a controlled workspace. Test protective functions with appropriately qualified personnel before exposing anyone to automatic motion. Regulatory requirements depend on the machine and location.

Useful metrics

Track cycle time distribution, success rate, mean repair time, intervention frequency and total operating cost. A fast demonstration that needs an engineer every few cycles may be less valuable than a slower reliable process.

Capstone evidence

Create a hazard log, interface specification, versioned configuration, fault-injection report and maintenance guide. Review upstream training branches: older ROS-Industrial material may target a different ROS distribution. Adapt and validate it, rather than mixing commands blindly.

quizzes.question: Can a successful ROS motion-planning demo be treated as a safety qualification?
options: No; safety functions and system validation are separate
Yes, after adding a warning label
quizzes.explanation: Functional behavior is not a safety certification.

lessons.title: Future-ready means testing ideas, not predicting magic
lessons.intro: Build the habit that survives changing frameworks.
lessons.body:
Choose a falsifiable question

Ask whether tactile sensing improves grasp recovery on a specified object set, or whether system-identification data improves transfer over broad randomization. Avoid questions such as "Can AI solve robotics?" that cannot guide a controlled experiment.

Read a paper in five passes

First identify the task and claimed contribution. Next inspect the assumptions. Then read the evaluation protocol and baselines. Study the implementation details. Finally write a reproduction plan including the missing information. A compelling video can hide careful resets or human interventions.

Promising directions, not promises

Contact-rich manipulation, uncertainty-aware perception, data quality, efficient adaptation and runtime monitoring are useful research directions. The latest named model is not automatically the right choice. Compare compute, latency, licensing, hardware compatibility and failure behavior.

An ablation is a deliberate removal

Run the same task with and without the proposed feature. Hold the budget and evaluation conditions constant. If performance does not change, the feature may not be doing what you thought, or your experiment may not distinguish its contribution.

Your research portfolio

Publish a baseline, an intervention, a controlled comparison and an honest limitation. Pin repository tags. Framework branches and model APIs move quickly; a reproducible result remains valuable after the names change.

quizzes.question: What is an ablation experiment?
options: Removing a component to measure its contribution
Making a larger logo for the result
Testing only the easiest successful trials
quizzes.explanation: A controlled removal helps isolate what a component actually contributes.

repos.name: ROBOTIS-GIT/turtlebot3
repos.description: Inspect a complete mobile-robot software stack.
repos.assignment: Trace description, sensor frames, odometry and navigation configuration. Match the ROS distribution branch.

repos.name: ros-navigation/navigation2
repos.description: Learn planners, costmaps, behavior trees and recovery.
repos.assignment: Log a failed route, explain the costmap and change one parameter at a time.

repos.name: moveit/moveit2
repos.description: Study planning scenes, kinematics and motion planning.
repos.assignment: Plan around an obstacle in simulation. Check collision geometry and controller interfaces before hardware execution.

repos.name: TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100
repos.description: Follow the SO-101 bill of materials, fit gauges and assembly.
repos.assignment: Identify servo voltage variants before ordering. Build one calibrated joint before the whole arm.

repos.name: huggingface/lerobot
repos.description: Explore demonstration datasets, training and deployment.
repos.assignment: Create episode-level splits and report task success separately from imitation loss.

repos.name: isaac-sim/IsaacLab
repos.description: Investigate native simulation and policy training.
repos.assignment: Pin a compatible release, train a supported task and replay the checkpoint separately. This website does not run Isaac Lab.

repos.name: ros-industrial/industrial_training
repos.description: Work through industrial robotics training material.
repos.assignment: Check distribution and branch; some training targets older ROS versions. Add safety and commissioning reviews for your use case.

repos.name: google-deepmind/mujoco
repos.description: Study a native physics simulator and model semantics.
repos.assignment: Modify a small MJCF model and check masses, joints, contacts and timestep convergence.

semesters.title: Foundation I
semesters.topics: Calculus, vectors, Python, units, measurement and DC circuits.
semesters.evidence: A measured circuit, unit tests and a reproducible experiment log.

semesters.title: Foundation II
semesters.topics: Linear algebra, differential equations, C/C++, digital logic and microcontrollers.
semesters.evidence: Firmware that handles stale data, input events and restart behavior.

semesters.title: Mechanics & signals
semesters.topics: Statics, dynamics, CAD, manufacturing, sampling, probability and electronics.
semesters.evidence: A serviceable mechanism and a controller with measured error.

semesters.title: Robotics core
semesters.topics: Kinematics, state estimation, camera geometry, control and Linux systems.
semesters.evidence: An evaluated vision system and a frame-consistent robot model.

semesters.title: Autonomy
semesters.topics: ROS 2, SLAM, motion planning, manipulation and distributed integration.
semesters.evidence: A navigation or manipulation system with reproducible failures.

semesters.title: Robot learning
semesters.topics: Optimization, reinforcement and imitation learning, datasets and evaluation.
semesters.evidence: A learned policy compared against a baseline on held-out tests.

semesters.title: Industry & specialization
semesters.topics: Real-time design, verification, industrial interfaces, safety and deployment.
semesters.evidence: A documented pilot, fault-injection results and operating-cost model.

semesters.title: Research & capstone
semesters.topics: Paper reproduction, controlled experiments, ethics, communication and teaching.
semesters.evidence: A reproducible technical report, portfolio and design defense.
